hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-20127 affecting Microsoft Exchange
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-20127 in Microsoft Exchange within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-20127; malware families: Cobalt Strike; threat actors: Volt Typhoon; vectors: exploit; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Microsoft Exchange
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Microsoft Exchange, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-20127.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Microsoft Exchange' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-20127 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-20127/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-20127 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-20127')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Microsoft Exchange hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Endpoint execution of Cobalt Strike
hypotheses.statement: One or more endpoints in the estate have executed or attempted to execute Cobalt Strike payloads since the reporting date.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'malware_execution' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-20127; malware families: Cobalt Strike; threat actors: Volt Typhoon; vectors: exploit; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: EDR hash sweep for Cobalt Strike
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a search of EDR file/process telemetry for known Cobalt Strike SHA256s returns zero hits in the last 90 days, payload presence is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process_events | where sha256 in (ti_lookup('Cobalt Strike', 'sha256')) | summarize count() by host

objectives.title: Behavioural pattern hunt for Cobalt Strike
objectives.falsification_criterion: If parent/child anomalies typical of the family (e.g. Office spawning script hosts, rundll32 chains) are absent across the estate, execution chain is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('winword.exe','excel.exe','outlook.exe') and child in ('rundll32.exe','wscript.exe','mshta.exe','powershell.exe')

objectives.title: Persistence-key inspection
objectives.falsification_criterion: If autoruns, scheduled tasks, services, and WMI subscriptions show no Cobalt Strike-aligned artifacts, post-execution persistence is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: registry_set | where key matches /Run|RunOnce|Image File Execution Options/ and value matches /unusual-path/

objectives.title: AV / quarantine retrospective
objectives.falsification_criterion: If retrospective AV / quarantine logs show no detections for related signatures over the last 30 days, the family is unlikely to have landed in-environment.
objectives.suggested_query: av_events | where signature contains 'Cobalt Strike' | summarize by host, action

objectives.title: Memory-resident loader check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a memory scan (YARA via EDR / Volatility) finds none of the published loader patterns on a sampled set of high-risk hosts, in-memory residency is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: memory_scan | yara_rule == 'rule_cobalt_strike' | summarize by host

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-20127; malware families: Cobalt Strike; threat actors: Volt Typhoon; vectors: exploit; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('rootfs.rw','libdssl.so','libcommon.so') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Post-foothold lateral movement consistent with Volt Typhoon
hypotheses.statement: An attacker who matched the TTPs of Volt Typhoon has moved laterally inside the estate using RDP/SMB/WinRM, admin tooling, or Kerberos abuse.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'lateral_movement' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-20127; malware families: Cobalt Strike; threat actors: Volt Typhoon; vectors: exploit; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: Anomalous remote logons (Type 3 / Type 10)
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4624 logon-type 3/10 events show no bursts from a single source to many destinations, lateral movement via RDP/SMB is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id in (4624) and logon_type in (3,10) | summarize dests = dcount(dst_host) by src_user, src_host | where dests > 10

objectives.title: Admin-tool usage outside baseline
objectives.falsification_criterion: If PsExec / WMIC / PowerShell remoting / Impacket-style usage is absent outside known admin jump-hosts, the lateral-tool hypothesis is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('psexec.exe','psexesvc.exe','wmic.exe','wsmprovhost.exe') and host !in (admin_jumphosts)

objectives.title: Kerberos abuse telemetry
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4769 ticket requests show no anomalous RC4 / odd-SPN patterns and no AS-REP roasting indicators, credential-based lateral movement is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id == 4769 and ticket_encryption == 'RC4-HMAC' | summarize by target_spn, account_name

objectives.title: Lateral file-copy staging
objectives.falsification_criterion: If SMB writes of archives / executables across multiple hosts from one user/host are absent, lateral staging is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: file | where action == 'write' and ext in ('.7z','.rar','.zip','.exe') and dest matches /\\\\.*\\(C\$|admin\$)/

article.title: NIK C2: The new AI-enabled command-and-control framework
article.summary: Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.”
article.raw_text: NIK C2: The new AI-enabled command-and-control framework Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.” Cisco Talos observed a new AI-integrated command-and-control (C2) framework in the wild called “NIK C2.” NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session. In this framework, the actor has abused the OpenAI Chat Completions application programming interface (API), which is a HTTP endpoint that enables ChatGPT-style conversations programmatically. In addition to the features that enable theft, an actor can also deploy desktop screen-locking ransomware via the NIK C2 implant onto the victim machine, leading to a ransom demand in Bitcoin or USDT cryptocurrencies. NIK C2 reshapes adversary tradecraft by collapsing collection and exploitation into a single continuous session, effectively erasing the offline processing delays that historically granted defenders critical detection windows. Such AI-enabled adversarial frameworks require defenders to move beyond traditional detection and embrace continuous behavioral vigilance as the new baseline. NIK C2 implant: AI-integrated remote access tool The NIK C2 implant is a Go-based, 64-bit Windows remote access tool that grants persistent control over compromised hosts using a resilient dual-channel C2 architecture. It communicates over TLS-secured WebSockets on port 443 alongside an HTTP fallback polling loop every 250 milliseconds, protecting all traffic with AES-256-GCM encryption derived from a hardcoded seed. To survive takedowns, the implant routes traffic across three prioritized C2 tiers, which are runtime-updated URLs, an embedded encrypted server list, and a hardcoded fallback address. Beyond standard operations, the implant features surveillance, theft, lateral movement, and evasion capabilities, including credential dumping, RDP session hijacking, process hollowing, and a C2-driven screen lock ransomware module. Notably, the NIK C2 implant embeds a fully integrated OpenAI API client via its ai_generate command, allowing operators to route arbitrary prompts to the OpenAI Chat Completions API directly through the infected host. The NIK C2 implant manages API key resolution, request assembly, and response parsing locally, returning the encrypted generative AI results to the actor's C2. The observed NIK C2 implant samples in the wild contains an embedded build path (/opt/nik_panel/data/build_52b79724a1fc4b8f/main.go), which identifies the project as "nik_panel" and indicates that the implant was cross compiled for Windows from a Linux development environment. Furthermore, the embedded eight-byte hex token matching the build identifier highlights that the threat actor's infrastructure actively tracking and versioning the implants. Figure 1. NIK C2 implant’s operational architecture. NIK C2 implant evolution timeline Talos observed that the NIK C2 implant development trajectory spans at least three distinct versions. All binaries observed in the wild were compiled with Go 1.23.4 (which was released in December 2024), placing the entire sample set compiled no earlier than late 2024. The actor has Zeroed PE TimeDateStamp fields and near-epoch filesystem timestamps (manifesting as Nov 29, 1979) are applied consistently across all samples. We developed a timeline based on the initial sighting dates of NIK C2 implant variants in OSINT. Figure 2. NIK C2 implant evolution timeline. The pace of capability addition across the three versions indicates a technically proficient team with prior malware operations experience is actively expanding NIK C2 towards a full-service adversarial framework. Active NIK C2 server seen in the wild During our research, we observed that a threat actor hosted the NIK C2 framework on a server at IP address “87.120.196[.]120”, resolving the domain “total-sitevv[.]lol”. The C2 server hosted an SSL/TLS certificate (serial number 7d16381a9de823943b5a0987dbd0f26edf22052b and jarm:"28d28d28d00000000042d42d0000001f361a1bf80ed39a1e352adeb016a07b" ) with the Common Name (CN) set to nik-panel . This CN value matches strings embedded within the implant binary. Observing the NIK C2 infrastructure active in the wild allowed us to assess with moderate confidence that NIK C2 is not merely a proof of concept, but a fully functional, AI-integrated C2 framework. Figure 3. NIK C2 was observed in the wild during the research period. NIK C2 implant integrates OpenAI’s API AI integration is one of the most architecturally distinct features of NIK C2 implant. It constructs a fully formed HTTP request to OpenAI’s production inference endpoint, transmits it from the victim machine IP address, parses the JSON response, and returns the AI-generated text to the actor’s panel. The entire operation from receiving the actor prompt to returning the large language model (LLM) reply is executed synchronously with a 60-second timeout. The implant begins by extracting three fields from the command payload received from the C2. The first field, identified by the key prompt , is the text the actor wants to send to the AI model. If the prompt string has zero length, the handler immediately constructs an error response and returns without making any outbound network call. The second field, identified by the key api_key is the OpenAI API key to use for authentication. The third field, identified by the key model , specifies which OpenAI model to use. Figure 4. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module. After extracting the three parameters, the implant checks whether the actor supplied an API key. If not, it calls the operating system's environment variable reader with the string OPENAI_API_KEY and uses the victim’s API key. This fallback is not a backup mechanism for API key resolution. It is a deliberate design with significant operational implications. If the victim has configured an OpenAI account on their machine, that account's API key will be used to fund the actor's AI inference. OpenAI's billing system will charge the victim's payment method, and OpenAI's access logs will show the victim's API key as the one that made the requests, allowing no trace attributable to the threat actor. If the actor does not specify a model name, the implant falls back to a five-character default string stored in the binary data section. Decoding the five-character value showed gpt-4 confirming that GPT4 is the default when no model is specified. The actor can override this by passing any valid OpenAI model identifier in the command payload, allowing selection of newer models as they become available without requiring a binary update. The implant builds the OpenAI API request body by constructing a map with four fields. The first field uses the key model and contains the resolved model name. The second field uses key messages and contains a two-element array of message maps. The third field uses the key temperature and contains a floating-point value read from a constant in the binary data section. The fourth field uses the key max_tokens and contains an integer value also read from binary. The message array is constructed in the order that the OpenAI Chat Completions API expects. The system message is first followed by the user message. The system message map has the role system and a content string that is exactly 68 bytes long hardcoded in the binary. This 68-byte string is the implant's behavioral instruction to the AI. It defines the model's operational role and response style for the duration of the session. The user message map has the role user and contains the actor's prompt text verbiage. The complete map structure is then serialized to JSON. The JSON message is sent to the URL https:// api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions , the OpenAI Chat Completions endpoint, through an HTTP POST request. Figure 5. Snippet of NIK C2 implant AI handler module. When the HTTP response arrives with a 200 status code, the handler uses Golang's JSON decoder to parse the response body directly into a generic map structure without defining a typed schema. It then navigates the decoded map by string key lookups in the sequence that the OpenAI Chat Completions API response structure defines. The outermost map is queried for the key choices which in a successful response contains an array. The implant checks that this array is non-empty, then accesses its element keys message and content . The string value at key content is the AI model-generated text response. After successfully extracting the AI-generated content, the handler assembles a result map with four entries. The key status is set to a constant string that reads as generated . The key code is set to the AI model's response text, so that the actor receives the full content of the model’s replies. The key model is set to the resolved model name that was used for the request, confirming which model produced the output. The key usage is set to the raw usage object from the OpenAI response, which contains the prompt token count, completion token count, and total token count. This usage data allows the actor to track how many tokens are consumed per request. The completed result map is ultimately transmitted to the C2 server over WebSocket or through the HTTP fallback C2 address. Figure 6. AI model response is encapsulated in JSON message and will be sent to C2. Dual execution modes of NIK C2 implant Upon execution, the implant inspects its command-line arguments to determine its execution path. The argument watchdog activates supervisory monitoring to relaunch the core process if terminated, the copywatchdog tracks file copy operations, and the absence of either defaults execution to primary agent mode. In primary mode, it uses a named mutex to enforce single-instance execution, logs a message reading [NIK] Starting , generates a 32-byte cryptographic session key if uninitialized, decodes its obfuscated C2 address, and sets its masquerade name to “svchost.exe” or “simvol.exe”. After initial setup, the binary records its process ID (PID) in the victim's temporary application folder and executes its persistence and evasion routines. These routines include copying to %appdata%/Roaming/Microsoft/Network with modified access controls, configuring Windows autostart registry entries, and masquerading its process. Finally, it starts the local proxy server, initiates the WebSocket communication loop in a separate goroutine, and enters a continuous heartbeat polling loop on the main thread. Implant’s C2 command surface overview The implant command dispatcher module facilitates over 52 commands that are directed by the C2 panel. The dispatcher module uses byte-level string matching to map the associated modules that are launched as concurrent goroutines, allowing multiple operations to run in parallel. The following table shows the NIK C2 implant’s command categories: Category Capability Description Stealer Credential Stealer Browser databases, saved passwords, cookies, autofill, crypto wallets, Discord tokens , Firefox profiles . Stealer Wi-Fi harvesting Extracts all saved WiFi SSIDs and plaintext passwords via Windows wireless configuration tooling . Surveillance Keylogger Real-time live stream per keystroke to actor panel, plus accumulated buffer dump on demand . Surveillance Screen Capture Full-screen screenshot and continuous screen stream . Surveillance Camera & Audio Camera snapshot and stream, microphone recording, live audio feed . Surveillance Clipboard Monitor Real-time clipboard content interception and replacement . Remote Control HVNC Hidden Virtual Network Computing — full desktop control invisible to the victim . Lateral Movement SOCKS5/HTTP Proxy Embedded proxy routing actor traffic through victim into internal network . Lateral Movement Reverse Proxy Tunnel Bidirectional TCP relay tunneled over C2 WebSocket for LAN pivoting . Lateral Movement RDP Operations RDP session interaction for lateral movement to other Windows hosts . Persistence Autostart & Masquerade Registry Run key persistence, process name masquerading, COM hijacking . Persistence Self-Heal Watchdog External watchdog subprocess monitors and relaunches agent on termination . Evasion Defense Bypass AMSI patch, debugger detection, stealth mode, UAC bypass, process hollowing . AI AI Generate Live OpenAI API inference routed through victim machine with actor prompts . Destructive Boot Ransomware Master Boot Record raw backup via PowerShell disk read and Screen- locking ransomware via LOLbin , registry persistence, crypto payment demand . Destructive Bootkit Preparation UEFI vs. BIOS detection, Secure Boot query, bootkit binary staging . Implant deploys screen-locking ransomware The ransomware module of the implant operates as a multi-stage attack controller that the actor runs in sequence to prepare, deploy, and retract a screen-locking ransomware payload. At first, it executes PowerShell to execute a raw disk copy command that reads directly from the physical drive device path (“\\.\PhysicalDrive0”) and writes the first sector, which is Master Boot Record (MBR), to a file named “mbr_backup.bin” in the Windows temporary directory. Figure 7. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s boot ransomware handler function. Next, the module constructs a complete self-contained HTML lock screen code entirely at runtime from a hardcoded format string, parameterized with actor supplied Bitcoin and USDT wallet addresses, prices, contact email, timer duration, and custom text from the C2 command message, allowing the actor to fully customize the ransom demands. Figure 8. Screenlocker HTML code is hardcoded in NIK C2 implant binary. After generating the HTML code, the binary writes it to the file “lock_screen.html” in the system temporary directory. It then generates a Windows batch script that calls mshta.exe with the path to the HTML file, followed by an infinite loop construct with a five-second timeout between iterations, ensuring that if the user somehow closes the window it reopens within five seconds. This batch file is written to the temp directory as “lock_start.bat”. The implant then runs a reg add command that writes a registry Run key named “SystemLock” under the current user's autostart path, pointing to a cmd /c invocation of the batch file, so the lock screen is executed on every user's logon. Additionally, a background goroutine is spawned that continuously monitors and relaunches the lock screen process. Finally, the module sends a confirmation response to C2 with the path of the deployed HTML file and the timer value. The design of this ransomware module is notable for several reasons. It does not encrypt any files, which means it leaves no forensic trail of file modification timestamps or encryption markers. It relies entirely on a screen lock, which is considerably faster to deploy than a file encryption ransomware. The persistence via registry Run key and a self-healing loop ensures the screen lock survives user attempts to dismiss it and survives a system restart. Figure 9. Desktop lockscreen page of the ransomware deployed by the NIK C2 implant. Implant’s bootkit preparation feature The bootkit preparation module of the implant is designed to survey the victim machine's boot firmware environment and then stage a bootkit payload file. It executes bcdedit /enum , the Windows Boot Configuration Data editor, with the output flag that enumerates all boot entries while hiding the console window. The implant reads the full output and searches for three specific substrings in sequence including EFI , Windows Boot Manager , and Windows Legacy OS Loader . If any of these are found, the boot type is classified as UEFI. The binary also searches for ntldr , the legacy Windows NT loader used by BIOS-mode systems as a fallback. Based on which string was matched, the boot type is recorded as either "UEFI" or "BIOS" as a string of the appropriate length. Separately, the binary runs a PowerShell command invoking Confirm-SecureBootUEFI , which is a built-in PowerShell command that returns to the current Secure Boot state. The output is searched for the string True to detect an enabled Secure Boot and for False to detect an explicitly disabled Secure Boot. If neither is present, the value is recorded as unknown . The result is sent back to the C2, a map containing the boot type classification and the Secure Boot status string. Then the implant writes a 16-byte placeholder file named “bootkit.bin” to the system temporary directory. The bytes written spell out "NIK_BOOTKIT_PREP" in ASCII, which serves as a staging marker rather than an actual bootkit binary. This placeholder confirms that the target path is writable by the current process, establishes the file location that subsequent operations will reference, and can be overwritten by the actual bootkit binary delivered through the implant's file-upload or file-write command handlers. The path to the staged file is returned to the C2 in response. Implant’s theft functionality When the actor issues the theft category commands from the C2, the implant executes the associated goroutines to collect the targeted data into a result map space in the victim machine memory: WiFi password theft (wifi_steal) The implant executes netsh commands directly via Go’s exec.Command function by passing arguments as discrete tokens rather than through a shell string. Harvested results are formatted under specific labels: plaintext Wi-Fi passwords appear under Key Content: , saved network names are cataloged under WiFi Profiles: (with missing entries flagged using the per-entry format [%s] not found ), and execution failures or absent interfaces return standardized error strings such as [WiFi] no wireless adapter or access denied and No WiFi profiles found . netsh wlan show profiles netsh wlan show profile name=" " key=clear Browser credential extraction (passwords, quick_steal) The implant stages targeted browser database files into an archive alongside the Local State file, which contains the AES master key protected by Data Protection Application Programming Interface (DPAPI). The implant imports and executes the CryptUnprotectData Windows API to unwrap the AES key and decrypt the databases locally. Otherwise, it exfiltrates the raw encrypted databases to the C2 server for offline extraction. Targeted browser database files are shown in the table: Browsers Targeted files Chrome Login Data, Cookies, Web Data, Local State, Bookmarks Edge Login Data, Cookies, Web Data, Local State Brave Login Data, Cookies, l eveldb file Opera Login Data from folder Opera Software\Opera Stable\ Firefox key4.db, logins.json , places.sqlite , formhistory.sqlite , Secure Preferences Token and cookie theft (token_grab, quick_steal) The implant extracts Discord tokens and session cookies from the levelDB store on the victim machine. The extracted outputs are labelled as === Discord Tokens === and DISCORD TOKENS . The browser session cookies (Discord_Cookies) are extracted from the copied Cookies database. Cryptocurrency wallet theft (crypto_steal, wallet_export) Victim’s desktop-based wallets are collected directly from the wallet storage paths. Browser extension wallets are extracted from chromium LevelDB stored by extension ID. Desktop based wallet storage paths targeted are listed below: /AppData/Roaming/Exodus/exodus.wallet /AppData/Roaming/Electrum/wallets /AppData/Local/Electrum/data/wallets /AppData/Roaming/Ethereum/keystore /AppData/Local/LedgerLive wallet.dat (Bitcoin Core) /AppData/Roaming/atomic (Atomic Wallet) Electrum\wallets Browser extension wallets targeted: Wallet Extension ID MetaMask (Chrome/Brave) nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn MetaMask (Edge) nkbihfbeogaeaoehlefnkodbefgpgknn Coinbase Wallet hnbohgpbmfldddohgoiefkeifpjficbk Phantom (Chrome) lnbcamaoebkogjmdnaofbeemigaalhlp Brave Wallet odbfpeeihodbihlmhbnhakoadhilfibh Seed phrase, private key file, and system reconnaissance The implant performs two regular expression patterns to search on the entire filesystem of the victim machine. These two regular expressions are designed to scan file names for sensitive cryptographic assets and credentials, functioning as case-insensitive patterns ?i . The first expression targets cryptocurrency recovery materials and wallet backups by matching keywords like "seed," "mnemonic," or "wallet" paired with common plain-text and data file extensions (.txt, .md, .csv, .dat), while the second seeks out asymmetric private keys and general secrets using terms like "private," "privkey," or "secret" paired with both text files and standard cryptographic key containers (.key, .pem). Because both patterns use unanchored, greedy matching (.*) without start (^) or end ($) boundary anchors, they capture any file where these sensitive terms precede the target extensions. Matched data are collected under the label of seed candidates and archived into “browserdata.zip”. (?i)(seed|phrase|mnemonic|recovery|backup|wallet).*(\.txt|\.md|\.csv|\.dat) (?i)(private|privkey|secret).*(\.txt|\.md|\.key|\.pem) The implant also performs victim machine reconnaissance by executing the following commands and uses chcp 65001 prefix to force the output in UTF-8 format. chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & systeminfo chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic os get lastbootuptime /value chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & wmic /namespace:\\root\SecurityCenter2 path AntiVirusProduct get displayName 2>nul chcp 65001 >nul 2>&1 & Get-Process | Select-Object Id, ProcessName | ConvertTo-Json -Compress After all collection paths are complete, the implant assembles all collected data into a single document that looks like a formatted report with clearly labeled sections for each data category such as === CRYPTO === , === WIFI === , === BROWSER === . Keylogger: Keystrokes livestreamed to C2 The keylogger module of the implant uses a persistent background goroutine that polls all 256 Windows virtual key codes, detecting keypresses via dynamically resolved API calls, and transmits the captured input. When a compromised victim presses a valid key on the keyboard, it is simultaneously streamed live as an AES-256-GCM encrypted JSON payload over WebSocket to C2 and also appends to an in-memory buffer capped at 10,000 entries and halved when full to prevent memory leaks. On an actor's dump command, this buffer is concatenated into a single string and returned to C2 via WebSocket or HTTP fallback, ensuring complete data transfer even during network interruptions. Stolen data exfiltration to C2 Once the archive is assembled, the entire result map is handed to the result transmission routine of the implant. That routine constructs a new JSON object containing five specific fields. It includes the command identifier echoed back from the original command. It also contains the agent's persistent identifier, formatted as ag_ . The type field is set to the string quick_steal_response . Finally, the data field holds the complete result map. Once constructed, this object is forwarded to the encryption routine. The routine serializes the object into JSON. It then generates 12 fresh random bytes to serve as a nonce. Next, it encrypts the serialized JSON using AES-256-GCM with a static key derived from a hardcoded seed. It concatenates the nonce, the ciphertext, and the 16-byte authentication tag and Base64-encodes the entire payload. The encrypted payload is placed in a wrapper object under the "e" key alongside the plain-text agent ID, and the wrapper is JSON marshaled into the final payload. This encrypted payload is then delivered through an available transmission path. The sending routine first checks whether the WebSocket connection is live. If it is, the payload is written directly into a WebSocket text frame on the existing connection, reaching the actor's panel with minimal latency. If the WebSocket is not currently connected, the routine falls back to an HTTP POST request to the endpoint path /api/c2/result on the C2 server, using the same encrypted body format. This dual-path design ensures stolen data is delivered even during WebSocket interruptions, as the HTTP channel remains functional independently of the WebSocket state. Implant’s C2 protocol The implant C2 architecture is designed for two independent, simultaneously operating communication channels. The primary channel is a persistent WebSocket connection over TLS. The secondary channel is an HTTP polling loop that posts to a fixed API endpoint at regular intervals. With the primary channel, the connection begins with a TCP dial to the C2 server address with an eight-second timeout. If the port is not explicitly present in the configured address, port 443 is appended automatically. Once the TCP socket is established, it is wrapped in a TLS session using a custom certificate configuration that pins to a specific certificate rather than validating against the system's certificate authority store. This prevents standard TLS interception proxies from observing traffic. Immediately after a successful WebSocket handshake but before any command is received, the implant transmits a full system registration message. The implant collects victim data such as the machine hostname, the local LAN IP address, the Windows username from the environment, a user security identifier, the local reverse-proxy port number that was assigned when the embedded proxy server was started, and the detected upstream proxy configuration derived from the Windows registry proxy settings. All of this is assembled into a JSON object and encrypted and sent to the C2. Figure 10. Snippet of NIK C2 IMPLANT’s C2 communication handler function. The HTTP polling channel runs independently. Every approximately 250 milliseconds, the agent collects a fresh snapshot of victim state hostname, watchdog status, local IP, username, current timestamp, and system uptime encrypts it in the same wire format and posts it to the /api/c2/update endpoint on the C2 server. Below table shows the C2 endpoints that the implant communicates: Endpoint Purpose / api /c2/update Reconnaissance beacon – victim system info / api /c2/result Command output exfiltration / api /c2/screen Screenshot upload / api /c2/ file_chunk File exfiltration / api /c2/ rproxy _up Reverse proxy upstream data / api /c2/ ws Websocket – a ctor command channel Every message on both channels, in both directions, uses the same symmetric encryption scheme. A hardcoded seed value stored in obfuscated form in the binary data section is decoded at startup and produces a 32-byte AES key. Decoded AES seed: d791dd0ff3228ed29a8d7333d4567be829159c5632ea347780992006f91c5295 32-byte AES key: 4887AFC0A574E9419A9695EF083460F58E4EF9A1C40793523CE112251273BDF9 The C2 server then responds with an encrypted payload, whose inner map contains a command array identical in structure to those delivered over WebSocket. Commands received through HTTP are dispatched through the same logic. If the HTTP POST fails, the agent rotates to the next server address before retrying. Figure 11. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s C2 communication handler function. The result transmission to the C2 is performed by the implant when a command handler completes its operation, the result is packaged into a response envelope containing the original command's identifier, the implant's own identifier, a type string formed by appending _response to the command name, the result data payload, and a top-level type marker of "result". This object is encrypted and delivered through either directly over the WebSocket connection if it is active, or via an HTTP POST to /api/c2/result . Implant’s defense evasion and anti-analysis techniques The NIK C2 implant deploys a layered set of defense evasion measures that activate immediately at startup and operate across the full compromise session. On launch, It hides its console window via API ShowWindow , renames the binary to “csrss.exe” in the Windows temp directory to impersonate a legitimate system process, disables Windows Recent Documents telemetry through a registry write action, and applies a critical-process flag via API NtSetInformationProcess with the parameter value 0x1D for ProcessBreakOnTermination that causes a Blue Screen of Death if any attempt is made to terminate the process through Task Manager or taskkill actions. Figure 12. Snippet of NIK C2 implant’s evasion handler module. Alongside these, two anti-debug checks IsDebuggerPresent and CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent run silently and call os.Exit(0) on detection, leaving no exception record or crash evidence. When directed by the C2, the implant can also escalate privileges without a UAC prompt using the fodhelper.exe COM hijack , which writes the implant path into HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\Shell\Open\command , triggers elevation, and cleans the registry key within two seconds. The implant bypasses the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) by executing a hardcoded, embedded PowerShell script that patches memory inside “System.Management.Automation.dll”. Specifically, it overwrites the AmsiInitFailed field with a six-byte stub (MOV EAX, E_INVALIDARG; RET) , forcing initialization to report failure and disabling content inspection for the remaining of the PowerShell session. Figure 13. NIK C2 Implant’s AMSI bypass PowerShell script. Conclusion The emergence of NIK C2, an AI-enabled command-and-control framework, underscores a critical shift in modern malware design: the transition from static intrusion toolsets to dynamic, modular implants that adapt on demand. By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, the compromised host is no longer a passive foothold but an autonomous operational asset. Operators can dynamically generate context-aware lure material, execute localized deception, synthesize operational intelligence, and craft targeted payloads directly on the compromised hosts — all while lowering the technical barrier which was traditionally required for such sophisticated tradecraft. Coverage The following ClamAV signature detects and blocks this threat: Win.Trojan.GoDiscorder-10060526-0 Indicators of compromise (IOCs) IOCs for this research can be found at our GitHub repository here .

hypotheses.title: Initial access via the disclosed vulnerability affecting Microsoft Exchange
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting the disclosed vulnerability in Microsoft Exchange within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on malware families: Cobalt Strike; vectors: phishing, exploit, rdp; impact: ransomware, fraud; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Microsoft Exchange
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Microsoft Exchange, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for the referenced CVE.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Microsoft Exchange' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for the referenced CVE in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-the referenced CVE/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the the referenced CVE fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('the referenced CVE')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Microsoft Exchange hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Endpoint execution of Cobalt Strike
hypotheses.statement: One or more endpoints in the estate have executed or attempted to execute Cobalt Strike payloads since the reporting date.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'malware_execution' selected based on malware families: Cobalt Strike; vectors: phishing, exploit, rdp; impact: ransomware, fraud; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: EDR hash sweep for Cobalt Strike
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a search of EDR file/process telemetry for known Cobalt Strike SHA256s returns zero hits in the last 90 days, payload presence is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process_events | where sha256 in (ti_lookup('Cobalt Strike', 'sha256')) | summarize count() by host

objectives.title: Behavioural pattern hunt for Cobalt Strike
objectives.falsification_criterion: If parent/child anomalies typical of the family (e.g. Office spawning script hosts, rundll32 chains) are absent across the estate, execution chain is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('winword.exe','excel.exe','outlook.exe') and child in ('rundll32.exe','wscript.exe','mshta.exe','powershell.exe')

objectives.title: Persistence-key inspection
objectives.falsification_criterion: If autoruns, scheduled tasks, services, and WMI subscriptions show no Cobalt Strike-aligned artifacts, post-execution persistence is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: registry_set | where key matches /Run|RunOnce|Image File Execution Options/ and value matches /unusual-path/

objectives.title: AV / quarantine retrospective
objectives.falsification_criterion: If retrospective AV / quarantine logs show no detections for related signatures over the last 30 days, the family is unlikely to have landed in-environment.
objectives.suggested_query: av_events | where signature contains 'Cobalt Strike' | summarize by host, action

objectives.title: Memory-resident loader check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a memory scan (YARA via EDR / Volatility) finds none of the published loader patterns on a sampled set of high-risk hosts, in-memory residency is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: memory_scan | yara_rule == 'rule_cobalt_strike' | summarize by host

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on malware families: Cobalt Strike; vectors: phishing, exploit, rdp; impact: ransomware, fraud; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('main.go','total-sitevv.lol','api.openai.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('87.120.196.120') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Post-foothold lateral movement consistent with the reported actor
hypotheses.statement: An attacker who matched the TTPs of the reported actor has moved laterally inside the estate using RDP/SMB/WinRM, admin tooling, or Kerberos abuse.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'lateral_movement' selected based on malware families: Cobalt Strike; vectors: phishing, exploit, rdp; impact: ransomware, fraud; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: Anomalous remote logons (Type 3 / Type 10)
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4624 logon-type 3/10 events show no bursts from a single source to many destinations, lateral movement via RDP/SMB is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id in (4624) and logon_type in (3,10) | summarize dests = dcount(dst_host) by src_user, src_host | where dests > 10

objectives.title: Admin-tool usage outside baseline
objectives.falsification_criterion: If PsExec / WMIC / PowerShell remoting / Impacket-style usage is absent outside known admin jump-hosts, the lateral-tool hypothesis is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('psexec.exe','psexesvc.exe','wmic.exe','wsmprovhost.exe') and host !in (admin_jumphosts)

objectives.title: Kerberos abuse telemetry
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4769 ticket requests show no anomalous RC4 / odd-SPN patterns and no AS-REP roasting indicators, credential-based lateral movement is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id == 4769 and ticket_encryption == 'RC4-HMAC' | summarize by target_spn, account_name

objectives.title: Lateral file-copy staging
objectives.falsification_criterion: If SMB writes of archives / executables across multiple hosts from one user/host are absent, lateral staging is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: file | where action == 'write' and ext in ('.7z','.rar','.zip','.exe') and dest matches /\\\\.*\\(C\$|admin\$)/

article.title: Inside a malicious Claude Code-branded extension and its persistent SSH backdoor
article.summary: Microsoft analyzes a malicious Claude Code–branded extension, its persistent SSH backdoor, and guidance to detect and remediate it. The post Inside a malicious Claude Code-branded extension and its persistent SSH backdoor appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .
article.raw_text: Inside a malicious Claude Code-branded extension and its persistent SSH backdoor Microsoft analyzes a malicious Claude Code–branded extension, its persistent SSH backdoor, and guidance to detect and remediate it. The post Inside a malicious Claude Code-branded extension and its persistent SSH backdoor appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog . In this article Attack chain overview Attack chain Host reconnaissance collection SSH authorization and tunnel identities Protocol Tunneling (T1572): reverse SSH forwarding Platform-specific startup persistence Mitigation and protection guidance Immediate actions Remediation actions Follow-up Investigation and recovery Microsoft Defender XDR detections Threat intelligence reports Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics Advanced hunting queries MITRE ATT&CK techniques Indicators of compromise (IOCs) Learn More On October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a tampered copy of Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code, versions 2.1.313 and 2.1.312) was available and served in the Cursor extension marketplace for a few hours to attempt a supply-chain attack on Cursor users. Cursor reports that it was live from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Daylight Time (PDT). We have confirmed that the malicious packages found on Cursor marketplace were never published nor distributed from Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and from npm @antropic-ai/claude-code, which were not affected by this incident. Anthropic confirmed to Microsoft that their systems were not compromised and they did not develop the malicious package posted in Cursor marketplace. At this time, all evidence suggests that the incident is limited to Cursor marketplace. Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed the injected JavaScript embedded in the malicious extension package. The injected loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled Secure Shell (SSH) key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence, and report host details. Successful remote access depends on host privileges, SSH configuration, and the attacker’s server configuration; however, the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when tunnel access fails. Organizations should identify systems that installed or automatically updated to this version from the Cursor marketplace, preserve evidence, remove confirmed malicious artifacts, review endpoint and network telemetry, and rotate credentials or revoke sessions when investigation indicates exposure. Microsoft customers can use the detections and hunting guidance in this post after the listed coverage and query validation gates are complete. Attack chain overview A malicious artifact associated with the Cursor Marketplace incident included a JavaScript function that executed before the extension’s expected code. When the module loads, this function can use Node.js APIs to collect host information, modify files, and execute operating-system commands. The following sections describe capabilities and attempted actions based on our analysis of the injected code. Attack chain The loader first collects host reconnaissance. It then attempts to install an SSH key, enable SSH, create a reverse tunnel, and configure persistence. A delayed callback subsequently attempts to send host details. The following sequence reflects code execution order; it does not prove that every step succeeded on every host. Module loading and reconnaissance collection. The injected function executes before normal extension initialization and collects host and user information. SSH access preparation. The loader appends an embedded public key and attempts to enable the local SSH service. Reverse forwarding. An embedded tunnel identity authenticates an outbound connection that requests forwarding to the workstation’s SSH port. Platform-specific persistence. Scripts and startup configuration are written to relaunch the connection. Host reconnaissance reporting. After the access and persistence setup attempts, a delayed callback attempts to transmit the previously collected host details and selected environment-variable names. Figure 1. Attack chain reconstructed from the injected code. The loader uses embedded components and built-in system tools to establish persistent access without downloading another executable. It suppresses command output and silently catches errors to conceal failures and malicious activity, while the extension continues functioning normally to avoid alerting users. Host reconnaissance collection The loader collects the hostname, username, operating system, architecture, home directory, working directory, and global Git email. It also looks for environment-variable names containing terms such as KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP, keeping up to forty matches. The callback sends matching environment-variable names, not values. This reveals potentially sensitive configuration categories but does not demonstrate theft of the secrets stored in those variables. Collection occurs during module loading. The collected details are retained for the delayed reporting callback described after the persistence stage. SSH authorization and tunnel identities The loader uses two SSH identities with distinct roles. One public key authorizes access to the workstation’s user account, while a separate private key authenticates the outbound connection to the tunnel server. First, the loader checks the user’s authorized_keys file for the comment svc-telemetry. If the marker is missing, it appends an embedded Ed25519 public key. That creates an authorization entry for whoever holds the corresponding private key, subject to the local SSH server’s configuration. Next, it decodes a separate private key for the outbound connection. The initial copy is written to a hidden temporary file named .stk_ followed by ten hexadecimal characters derived from the hostname and home directory. SSH receives that file through its -i option and connects using the remote account tunnel. The public-key material is redacted but the format is similar to the following: ssh-ed25519 [REDACTED PUBLIC KEY] svc-telemetry Protocol Tunneling (T1572): reverse SSH forwarding The tunneling SSH process is launched with the command line containing the following arguments: -N -R '*:0:localhost:22' It requests a listening port on the remote SSH server and forwards connections through the tunnel to port 22 on the victim’s loopback interface. The remote port value 0 asks the server to allocate a port; it does not change the local target from port 22. The -N option tells SSH not to run a command on the tunnel server. This design starts with an outbound connection from the workstation rather than waiting for a direct inbound connection to it. The loader disables ordinary host-key checking, bypasses the normal known-hosts file, sets keepalives, and avoids interactive prompts. On Unix-like systems it prefers autossh, falling back to ssh; on Windows it uses a hidden PowerShell loop. The loops wait sixty seconds after SSH exits before retrying. Figure 2. Terminal-style SSH command configuring an outbound reverse tunnel from a server-assigned remote port to the workstation’s local SSH service on port 22. Host-key verification is disabled, and the identity-file path is redacted. A running SSH process does not necessarily mean the attacker gained access. Both the attacker’s server and the victim’s workstation must allow the connection, and server settings determine whether the tunnel is publicly reachable. Cursor reports that errors and administrator-permission requirements blocked SSH access on most macOS and Windows hosts. However, the malware could still attempt to plant its SSH key, establish persistence, and report host information. Platform-specific startup persistence The loader writes platform-specific scripts and startup configuration outside the extension directory. The following table summarizes these mechanisms and their associated artifacts. The code attempts to configure persistence, but the presence of an artifact alone does not establish that the startup mechanism ran successfully. Platform Startup mechanism Key artifacts macOS User LaunchAgent with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist, ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk Linux User-crontab @reboot entry ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk Windows Attempted SysMon scheduled task requesting SYSTEM execution %USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd, %USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk Windows fallback Batch file in the user’s Startup folder %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\sysmon.cmd On Unix-like systems, the .smt script reconstructs the persistent .smtk identity when it runs, then starts its own SSH retry loop. On Windows, the loader writes the identity and batch script directly. The startup objects use names such as SysMon and com.apple.sysmond, which resemble monitoring components. Behind these names, their configured actions invoke the generated scripts that maintain reverse SSH forwarding. Mitigation and protection guidance Immediate actions Run advanced hunting queries below to identify affected systems and investigate systems where users installed or automatically updated anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.313 and 2.1.312 through the Cursor Extension Marketplace. Review extension-installation records and correlate endpoint, network, file, process, and authentication telemetry with the published indicators. Preserve the extension package, modified SSH authorization files, generated keys and scripts, and startup configuration before cleanup. Isolate devices with evidence of loader execution or backdoor installation. Remediation actions After evidence collection, check the affected user’s ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on macOS and Linux for the attacker-controlled key labeled svc-telemetry. On Windows, check both %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\authorized_keys and C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys, where present. Confirm the key against the fingerprint in Indicators of Compromise before removing the exact unauthorized entry. Preserve unrelated SSH keys and legitimate remote-development configuration. A missing marker alone should not replace review of the installation, process, network, and persistence evidence. Remove the trojanized extension and confirmed malicious persistence after evidence collection. Inspect each startup object’s configured action before removal; names alone are not sufficient to distinguish malicious objects from legitimate monitoring software. macOS: Unload and remove the malicious user LaunchAgent at ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist and remove its associated ~/.config/.smt script and ~/.config/.smtk identity. Linux: Remove the malicious user-crontab @reboot entry referencing ~/.config/.smt, preserving unrelated entries, and remove the associated script and ~/.config/.smtk identity. Windows: Remove the malicious SysMon scheduled task, the Startup-folder sysmon.cmd fallback, and associated %USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd and %USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk files. All applicable platforms: Stop confirmed malicious SSH and retry processes and remove their temporary .stk_ identity files after collection. Cursor published platform-specific checks and remediation scripts in its security notice . Review the scripts and execution requirements before use, then verify that no listed artifacts remain. Cleanup does not replace investigation of device activity during the exposure window. Removing or updating the extension does not remove artifacts written outside its installation directory. Remove confirmed unauthorized SSH keys, tunnel identities, scripts, and startup entries separately. Cursor’s reported server takedown does not remove artifacts already present on a device. Follow-up Investigation and recovery Review telemetry after the extension loaded for SSH key acceptance, tunnel processes, local SSH sessions, command execution, and file activity. Rotate credentials and revoke sessions from a known-clean device when telemetry indicates credential access or when device trust cannot be restored. Rebuild the device when required by the investigation and verify that the tunnel and startup artifacts do not return after login or restart. To reduce the risk of malicious extensions and extension-based supply chain attacks, organizations using Cursor should apply the relevant controls in Cursor’s security-hardening guidance , including restricting extensions to approved publishers and configuring an extension installation cooldown to delay installation of newly published versions. These measures can help limit exposure to malicious releases. Microsoft Defender XDR detections Microsoft Defender XDR customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender XDR coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. Customers with provisioned access can also use Microsoft Security Copilot in Microsoft Defender to investigate and respond to incidents, hunt for threats, and protect their organization with relevant threat intelligence. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments. Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics Activity Profile: Malicious Claude Code branded extension v2.1.313 contains a persistent SSH backdoor Advanced hunting queries The following queries use the Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting schema and the time range selected in the portal. A result is an investigative lead, not proof of compromise. Connections to the reported infrastructure Find network events involving the reported IP address during the last 30 days, including the process responsible for each connection. DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteIP == "134.209.82.225" or RemoteUrl has "134.209.82.225" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl Reported malicious file and persistence artifacts Find file events matching the reported SHA-256 hash, artifact filenames, or filename prefix during the last 30 days. Filename matches are hunting leads and require investigation. DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 == "ecb58cb29078d9646ad1dcdbe51526f2d9cfea06be5fb2ab183e8ecc3ab6bf15" or FileName in~ ( ".smt", ".smtk", "smt.cmd", "smtk", "sysmon.cmd", "com.apple.sysmond.plist" ) or FileName startswith ".stk_" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine SHA-256 values might not be populated for every file event. The filename and prefix conditions provide additional hunting leads. Possible Windows scheduled-task persistence Find scheduled-task creation events whose additional fields contain both reported terms, SysMon and smt, during the last 30 days. DeviceEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated" | where AdditionalFields has "SysMon" and AdditionalFields has "smt" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine Possible macOS LaunchAgent persistence Find plist-property modification events whose FolderPath matches the reported com.apple.sysmond.plist artifact. DeviceEvents | where ActionType == "PlistPropertyModified" | where FolderPath has "com.apple.sysmond.plist" MITRE ATT&CK techniques The following mappings describe behaviors implemented or attempted by the analyzed loader, not confirmed execution on every affected host. They do not establish attribution to a particular threat actor. Technique Code behavior T1098.004 – SSH Authorized Keys Adds an embedded public key to the user’s authorization file. T1572 – Protocol Tunneling Requests reverse SSH forwarding to the workstation’s local SSH service. T1053.003 – Cron Attempts a Linux user-crontab @reboot entry. T1053.005 – Scheduled Task Attempts a Windows startup task requesting SYSTEM execution. hypotheses.title: Initial access via the disclosed vulnerability affecting Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting the disclosed vulnerability in Microsoft 365 / Entra ID within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on malware families: Cobalt Strike; vectors: phishing, supply-chain; impact: fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for the referenced CVE.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Microsoft 365 / Entra ID' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for the referenced CVE in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-the referenced CVE/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the the referenced CVE fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('the referenced CVE')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Microsoft 365 / Entra ID hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Endpoint execution of Cobalt Strike
hypotheses.statement: One or more endpoints in the estate have executed or attempted to execute Cobalt Strike payloads since the reporting date.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'malware_execution' selected based on malware families: Cobalt Strike; vectors: phishing, supply-chain; impact: fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: EDR hash sweep for Cobalt Strike
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a search of EDR file/process telemetry for known Cobalt Strike SHA256s returns zero hits in the last 90 days, payload presence is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process_events | where sha256 in (ti_lookup('Cobalt Strike', 'sha256')) | summarize count() by host

objectives.title: Behavioural pattern hunt for Cobalt Strike
objectives.falsification_criterion: If parent/child anomalies typical of the family (e.g. Office spawning script hosts, rundll32 chains) are absent across the estate, execution chain is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('winword.exe','excel.exe','outlook.exe') and child in ('rundll32.exe','wscript.exe','mshta.exe','powershell.exe')

objectives.title: Persistence-key inspection
objectives.falsification_criterion: If autoruns, scheduled tasks, services, and WMI subscriptions show no Cobalt Strike-aligned artifacts, post-execution persistence is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: registry_set | where key matches /Run|RunOnce|Image File Execution Options/ and value matches /unusual-path/

objectives.title: AV / quarantine retrospective
objectives.falsification_criterion: If retrospective AV / quarantine logs show no detections for related signatures over the last 30 days, the family is unlikely to have landed in-environment.
objectives.suggested_query: av_events | where signature contains 'Cobalt Strike' | summarize by host, action

objectives.title: Memory-resident loader check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a memory scan (YARA via EDR / Volatility) finds none of the published loader patterns on a sampled set of high-risk hosts, in-memory residency is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: memory_scan | yara_rule == 'rule_cobalt_strike' | summarize by host

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on malware families: Cobalt Strike; vectors: phishing, supply-chain; impact: fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('anthropic.claude','node.js','com.apple.sysmond.plist') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('134.209.82.225') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

article.title: EPICS Base
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to cause a denial-of-service condition, corrupt memory, disclose sensitive information, or potentially execute arbitrary code. The following versions of EPICS Base are affected: EPICS Base release CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.8 The EPICS Community EPICS Base release 3 Vulnerabilities Integer Overflow or Wraparound, Improper Handling of Length Parameter Inconsistency, Access of Resource Using Incompatible Type ('Type Confusion') Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Global Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-114595 In EPICS Base release 7.0.10 and prior, an integer overflow in network request processing can cause memory to be allocated with an incorrect size. Subsequent handling of attacker supplied data may result in memory corruption, denial of service, or potential remote code execution. Read More 1 Affected Product The EPICS Community EPICS Base release: Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation The EPICS Community has made available updates to the epics-base GitHub repositories. Affected users should update to the 7.0.11 release. For more information, users should contact the EPICS Controls team https://epics-controls.org/support/. Mitigation https://github.com/epics-base/epics-base/pull/934 Mitigation https://github.com/epics-base/epics-base/pull/937 Mitigation https://githu

Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.
