objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-114595/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-114595 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-114595')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-114595, CVE-2026-114596, CVE-2026-114597; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge; impact: ddos.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('epics-controls.org') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-114595, CVE-2026-114596, CVE-2026-114597; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge; impact: ddos.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths
article.summary: Teams support impersonation led to remote access, malicious runtime execution, and Certificate Services abuse through authentication relay and Kerberos. The post From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .
article.raw_text: From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths Teams support impersonation led to remote access, malicious runtime execution, and Certificate Services abuse through authentication relay and Kerberos. The post From help desk impersonation to AD CS abuse: Investigating ESC1 and ESC8 intrusion paths appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog . In this article Activity overview Attack chain overview Portable runtime staging and execution variants Host discovery and AD CS assessment Case 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusion Case 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identity Why the response outcomes differed Actionable investigation methods References Learn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence investigated two human-operated intrusions in which threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist. Once connected, the threat actors staged portable Python, Bun, or Java runtimes, performed host and network discovery, and assessed Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) for certificate-based authentication paths. Although the incidents began with the same social-engineering and remote-access pattern, they diverged at the certificate layer. In Case 1, the threat actor abused an Enterprise CA Security Configuration 1 (ESC1) -vulnerable certificate template to obtain authentication certificates for privileged accounts and performed DCSync. In Case 2, the threat actor used PetitPotam, a technique that causes a Windows server to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system. The attacker relayed the domain controller’s New Technology (NT) LAN Manager (NTLM) authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment (ESC8), obtained a certificate for the domain-controller account, and used it for certificate-based Kerberos authentication (PKINIT – Public Key Cryptography for Initial Authentication). This intrusion pattern is high impact because a user-approved remote session can become certificate-backed access to privileged identities and domain infrastructure. In Case 1, Microsoft Defender attack disruption restricted covered identities and blocked substantial follow-on activity, but a privileged identity excluded from automated containment remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. In Case 2, Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the associated workstation and no further progression was observed. The activity did not exploit a vulnerability in Microsoft Teams; instead, it relied on social engineering and insecure or overly permissive AD CS configurations. In this blog, we analyze the shared attack chain, the ESC1 and ESC8 certificate-abuse paths, and the different response outcomes. We also provide investigation methods, mitigation recommendations, Microsoft Defender detection guidance, and advanced hunting queries to help defenders identify and interrupt this access path. The activity described here is not attributed to a specific threat actor. Activity overview Risk to enterprise environments AD CS can turn a certificate request into a durable authentication path. An attacker who obtains an authentication certificate for a privileged user or machine account can use that certificate independently of the initially compromised password. Resetting the user’s password or reimaging the first workstation does not revoke an issued certificate or invalidate Kerberos tickets that have already been issued. Two AD CS abuse techniques are central to these incidents: ESC1 – certificate template abuse: A low-privileged requester abuses a misconfigured authentication-capable template that permits requester-supplied identity information and broad enrollment, allowing the requester to obtain a certificate for a privileged account. ESC8 – NTLM relay to Web Enrollment: An attacker relays a user or machine account’s NTLM authentication to an AD CS web enrollment endpoint that lacks relay protections, then requests a certificate as the relayed identity. Attackers can use Microsoft Teams to impersonate IT support personnel and persuade users to approve a remote session, gaining hands-on-keyboard access without a conventional malware attachment. Portable or renamed runtimes such as Python, Bun, and Java can execute attacker-controlled scripts from user-writable locations while retaining legitimate file metadata. Automated disruption is most effective when every compromised identity and device remains eligible for containment; exclusions can preserve the attacker’s path. Attack chain overview Both incidents followed the same initial sequence: help desk impersonation through Teams, a user-approved Quick Assist or other remote-support session, archive transfer and extraction, portable runtime execution, and host and AD CS discovery. The certificate technique and response outcome then split into two distinct branches. Figure 1. Both incidents followed a shared entry and execution pattern before diverging into two AD CS abuse paths. Case 1 used an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template to obtain certificates for privileged identities. Case 2 used PetitPotam to coerce domain-controller authentication and relay it to AD CS Web Enrollment through ESC8. The response outcomes differed based on containment coverage and removal of the active execution point. Shared initial access and execution pattern Teams helpdesk impersonation and remote access Both incidents began with Teams phishing messages and calls that impersonated support personnel. The social engineering persuaded a user to establish an attacker-controlled remote session , primarily by guiding the user to open Quick Assist and provide the connection code. This gave the attacker hands-on-keyboard access to the workstation. Across the broader activity, organization-themed onmicrosoft.com tenant names and support-oriented display names were used to make the external contact appear familiar. Figure 2. Example Teams call displaying External and Scam suspected indicators. These labels are important user-facing signals during support impersonation attempts. The remote session was the decisive transition in the attack. Immediately after the user granted control through Quick Assist, the attacker used the session to place an archive in the victim’s Downloads folder. Commands launched during the session created a KB-prefixed staging directory under the user’s profile, extracted the archive into that directory, and started the included payload with a portable Python, JavaScript, or Java runtime. The payload then performed host and network discovery and began assessing AD CS. Portable runtime staging and execution variants The runtime and packaging varied between deployments, but the execution pattern remained consistent: an archive was placed on the device during the remote session, extracted into a newly created user-profile directory, and used to launch attacker-controlled code. In one JavaScript variant, a renamed executable retained version metadata identifying it as the Bun runtime and launched the staged loader. A separate variant used a staged Java runtime to launch a Java source file. Figure 3. Sanitized Bun staging command. The update-themed path, renamed runtime, script operand, and remote-session context form the useful investigation pattern. File names alone are weak indicators. The actionable pattern is a portable runtime launched from a newly created, user-writable staging directory after an unauthorized remote session, followed by script execution, discovery commands, or connections to identity infrastructure. Figure 4. Sanitized Java staging variant. The campaign could substitute runtime and packaging choices while keeping the broader access pattern. The Java variant confirms that runtime choice can change between deployments. The AD CS behavior in each incident should be validated through the initiating process, account, device, and certificate records rather than assumed from the presence of Bun or Java alone. Host discovery and AD CS assessment The staged components queried Windows version information, network configuration, and running processes. These commands are common in administration, but they become high-value signals when it is launched by a renamed runtime from an uncommon location and follow an unexpected remote-support session. Figure 5. Host-discovery commands from the first draft. Their value comes from the initiating staged runtime, user-writable path, and preceding unauthorized remote session. The compromised workstation also connected to domain infrastructure using LDAPS and SMB. From this shared workstation foothold, the incidents followed different certificate-abuse paths. In Case 1, the attacker exploited an ESC1-vulnerable certificate template. In Case 2, the attacker used PetitPotam to coerce domain-controller authentication and relay it to AD CS Web Enrollment through ESC8. Case 1: ESC1 abuse and the cost of an identity exclusion ESC1 certificate requests expand privilege The first Teams-phishing wave targeted three user accounts and compromised one workstation. From the shared foothold described above, the attacker examined AD CS for a privilege-escalation path. Figure 6. Case 1: Help desk impersonation led to ESC1 certificate abuse. Attack disruption restricted most compromised identities, but an excluded privileged account remained usable and later supported data exfiltration. The attacker found a certificate template vulnerable to ESC1. ESC1 describes a template configuration in which a requester can supply identity information in the certificate request and obtain a certificate that supports authentication. When broad enrollment rights and weak issuance controls are combined with that setting, a low-privileged account can request a certificate representing a privileged identity. In the first wave, the attacker obtained certificates for three highly privileged accounts. Microsoft Defender attack disruption targeted the initially compromised user and those three certificate-compromised identities. Remote logons and Server Message Block (SMB) access were restricted and active sessions were disconnected. One privileged account was excluded from automated response, so containment did not apply to that identity. Renewed phishing and ESC1 privilege expansion About 90 minutes after the first disrupted session, the attacker launched a larger Teams-phishing wave targeting 16 users and compromised another workstation. The attacker again abused the ESC1-vulnerable template, this time obtaining certificates for eight additional privileged accounts. Attack disruption targeted the newly compromised user and the eight certificate-compromised identities. More than 1,000 subsequent SMB file-access attempts and additional logon attempts were blocked, limiting the attacker’s ability to reuse those accounts for lateral movement. DCSync, the excluded account, and data theft Within seconds of obtaining one privileged certificate, the attacker authenticated to a domain controller and performed DCSync while containment was taking effect. Attack disruption limited additional replication and follow-on use, but the operation had already begun. The privileged account excluded during the first disruption remained available. The attacker continued to use it for network and remote-interactive logons, reached a file server, and launched a renamed copy of Rclone using the filename SearchApp.exe. The command recursively copied data from a file-server share to an external Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) destination, used 20 concurrent transfers, selected files up to three years old, and excluded several executable, database, virtual-disk, media, temporary, and log file types. Figure 7. Sanitized Rclone command used to copy data from a file-server share to an external SFTP destination. The incident demonstrates that partial identity containment can reduce attack activity while still leaving a viable privileged route. Case 2: PetitPotam and ESC8 turn a workstation into a domain-controller identity PetitPotam coerces domain-controller authentication The ESC1 path used in the first case was not available in this environment. Instead, the attacker used PetitPotam to send requests over the Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (EFSRPC), causing the domain controller to authenticate to an attacker-controlled system using its machine account. The attacker then relayed that NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment without knowing the domain controller’s password. Figure 8. Case 2: Help desk impersonation led to PetitPotam authentication coercion, ESC8 relay to AD CS, certificate-based Kerberos authentication, and customer-led device isolation. NTLM relay reaches AD CS Web Enrollment The attacker relayed the domain controller’s NTLM authentication to AD CS Web Enrollment. This technique is known as ESC8. It targets an enrollment web endpoint that accepts NTLM without sufficient relay protection, allowing the attacker to submit a certificate request as the relayed account. The AD CS server authenticated the domain-controller machine account even though the connection originated from another device. That identity-to-source mismatch is a strong investigation pivot: correlate the machine account, source device, Web Enrollment request, Certification Authority (CA) issuance record, and subsequent Kerberos activity. After authenticating to Web Enrollment as the domain controller, the attacker requested and retrieved a certificate using the Domain Controller template. The important service paths are the certificate submission and retrieval endpoints under /certsrv; isolated URL access is not malicious by itself and must be correlated with the authenticated identity, source device, process, and CA request. Figure 9. Sanitized view of AD CS Web Enrollment activity involving certificate submission and retrieval through /certsrv, used during ESC8 certificate issuance for a relayed domain-controller identity. Certificate-based Kerberos authentication The attacker used the newly issued domain-controller certificate for Kerberos PKINIT and obtained a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) for the domain controller. This step converted a relayed NTLM authentication into a certificate-backed Kerberos identity. PKINIT success is the response threshold: responders should investigate the requesting device, authenticated account, issued certificate, active Kerberos sessions, and any service-ticket use. Certificate revocation and Kerberos ticket review are separate containment actions. Customer-led device isolation and observed outcome Microsoft Defender generated ESC8-related alerts, after which the customer isolated the workstation associated with the certificate-enrollment and Kerberos activity. The documented containment action in this case was customer-led device isolation. No further attack progression was observed following isolation. Why the response outcomes differed In Case 1, an exclusion left a compromised privileged account available to the attacker despite disruption of other identities. In Case 2, customer-led device isolation followed Defender alerts, and no further attack progression was observed. Response element Case 1: ESC1 Case 2: ESC8 Response mechanism Microsoft Defender automated attack disruption targeting compromised identities. Microsoft Defender alerts followed by customer-led device isolation. Measured effect Covered identities were restricted; more than 1,000 SMB attempts and additional logons were blocked; further DCSync activity was limited. The workstation associated with certificate enrollment and Kerberos activity was isolated. Containment follow-up One privileged account was excluded from automated response and remained available to the attacker. No further progression was observed after isolation; Observed outcome The excluded identity was later used for file-server access and data exfiltration. No subsequent attack progression was documented after customer isolation. Actionable investigation methods The most useful artifacts are not individual commands or ports in isolation. Investigators should reconstruct the chain across collaboration, endpoint, identity, and certificate systems. Teams and remote access: identify the external tenant, user interaction, call or chat timing, remote-session start, approved remote monitoring and management (RMM) process, and child processes created during the session. Runtime staging: inspect newly created KB-prefixed or application-like folders, archive extraction, runtime metadata, script operands, parent-child relationships, and subsequent network activity. Directory interaction: use network data to identify LDAPS and SMB connections, then use endpoint and directory logs to determine what the initiating process did. TLS intentionally hides LDAP query content from passive network inspection. ESC1: review certificate request and issuance events, requester identity, subject and Subject Alternative Names (SAN) values, template name, enrollment permissions, and the first authentication performed with the issued certificate. PetitPotam and ESC8: correlate EFSRPC activity, outbound authentication by the domain controller, the device that relayed the authentication, Web Enrollment access, CA request and issuance records, and PKINIT from the originating workstation. Disruption and containment: enumerate every compromised identity and device, review exclusions before and during response, revoke unauthorized certificates, and assess active Kerberos tickets separately Reduce support impersonation and unauthorized remote access Require users to verify unsolicited support requests through a known internal channel before joining a call, sharing a screen, or starting a remote-control session. Encourage users to pay attention to warnings in incoming messages and calls when impersonation is detected. Review Teams external-access and federation policies. Limit external domains to business requirements and investigate newly observed organization-themed or helpdesk-themed tenants in context. Restrict remote-support software to approved products, operators, and workflows. Alert when approved RMM tools extract archives, create interpreters, or launch scripts from user-writable paths. Constrain runtime-based execution Use App Control for Business or equivalent application control to restrict unapproved portable runtimes and script execution from user-writable locations. Evaluate file identity through signer, original filename, product metadata, path, parent process, and behavior. A renamed executable can retain legitimate version information. Test relevant attack surface reduction rules and endpoint protection policies. Do not assume controls for Windows script hosts automatically cover JavaScript executed through Bun or source files launched through Java. Harden AD CS against ESC1 and ESC8 Follow Microsoft’s secure configuration guidance for mitigating NTLM relay against AD CS: https://support.microsoft.com/help/5005413 Review authentication-capable templates for requester-supplied subject information, broad enrollment permissions, weak issuance requirements, and excessive certificate purpose. Remove unnecessary enrollment rights and require approval where appropriate. Inventory AD CS Web Enrollment and Certificate Enrollment Web Service endpoints. Remove endpoints that are not required. Require HTTPS and enforce Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on enrollment web endpoints. HTTPS protects confidentiality; EPA provides the channel binding needed to resist NTLM relay. Disable NTLM on enrollment services where operationally feasible and validate Kerberos-only authentication before broad enforcement. Use Defender for Identity AD CS security posture assessments to identify ESC1-related template exposure and insecure enrollment Internet Information Services (IIS) endpoints associated with ESC8: https://learn.microsoft.com/defender-for-identity/security-posture-assessments/certificates Enable certificate auditing and prepare certificate-aware response Enable the Certification Services advanced audit subcategory for success and failure, and configure the Certification Authority audit filter to record request and issuance activity. Preserve CA security events, CA database records, IIS or Web Enrollment logs, endpoint process lineage, identity alerts, and Teams interaction records. If an unauthorized certificate was issued, identify its serial number and thumbprint, revoke it, publish updated revocation information, and confirm that relying systems can obtain the update. Review certificate-based Kerberos activity and active tickets. Revoking a certificate does not retroactively invalidate TGTs or service tickets that were already issued. Treat containment exclusions as incident decisions. If an account or device cannot be automatically contained, assign a compensating manual action and verify completion. Microsoft Defender XDR detections and disruption Microsoft Defender XDR can connect collaboration, endpoint, identity, certificate, and Kerberos signals. Alert names and availability depend on product configuration and enabled sensors. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Possible initial access from an emerging threat – Suspicious JavaScript process Discovery Staged runtimes query host configuration and interact with domain infrastructure. Useful prompts should ask for the initiating device, remote-session context, certificate request, issued identity, PKINIT activity, and any response exclusions. Results depend on connected plugins, permissions, and the evidence available to the incident. Threat intelligence reports Microsoft customers can use Microsoft Defender XDR Threat Analytics to review relevant reports, related incidents, impacted assets, and recommended actions. Search for Teams support impersonation, portable Bun or Java runtimes, AD CS certificate abuse, NTLM relay, ESC1, ESC8, and certificate-based Kerberos authentication. Campaign-specific report. Advanced hunting Use these queries to investigate related activity. Tune time windows and filters for your environment. Matches require investigation. Teams external contact and available impersonation signals Use these queries as investigation starting points. Validate field availability and expected values in your tenant, tune for legitimate activity, and correlate matches with incidents rather than treating a single result as proof of compromise. DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "bun.exe" or FileName in~ ("bun.exe", "java.exe", "javaw.exe") | where ProcessCommandLine contains ".js" or ProcessCommandLine contains ".java" | where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\AppData\\Roaming\\KB[0-9]+\\" | order by Timestamp desc Network activity initiated by the staged runtime Find network connections initiated by the staged runtime. DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "bun.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ( "bun.exe", "java.exe", "javaw.exe") | where RemotePort in (80, 445, 636, 88) | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath matches regex @"(?i)\\AppData\\Roaming\\KB[0-9]+\\" | order by Timestamp desc Enrollment, relay, and PKINIT alerts with their evidence Find relay, AD CS, and PKINIT alerts with their related evidence. hypotheses.title: Initial access via the disclosed vulnerability affecting Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting the disclosed vulnerability in Microsoft 365 / Entra ID within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, smb; impact: data-breach, fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, Active Directory.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for the referenced CVE.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Microsoft 365 / Entra ID' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for the referenced CVE in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-the referenced CVE/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the the referenced CVE fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('the referenced CVE')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Microsoft 365 / Entra ID hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, smb; impact: data-breach, fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, Active Directory.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('onmicrosoft.com','searchapp.exe','support.microsoft.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Data staging and exfiltration to attacker-controlled storage
hypotheses.statement: Sensitive data has been staged (archived) and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled endpoints or cloud-storage tenants in the reporting window.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'exfiltration' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, smb; impact: data-breach, fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, Active Directory.

objectives.title: Cloud-storage exfil to non-corp tenants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If DLP / proxy show no uploads to mega.nz, anonfiles, transfer.sh, or personal Dropbox/OneDrive tenants, cloud exfil is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: proxy | where host matches /mega\.nz|anonfiles\.com|transfer\.sh|filebin\.net/ | summarize bytes = sum(bytes_out) by user

objectives.title: Archive-then-egress pattern
objectives.falsification_criterion: If user/host telemetry shows no archive creation (rar/7z) within minutes of a large outbound transfer, the stage-then-exfil pattern is absent.
objectives.suggested_query: file_create | where ext in ('.rar','.7z','.zip') | join (egress | where bytes_out > 50MB) on host within 30m

objectives.title: Outbound volume to rare ASNs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If outbound bytes-by-ASN over the last 30 days show no first-seen / low-reputation destination receiving >1GB, bulk exfil is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: netflow | summarize bytes = sum(bytes_out) by asn | where asn !in (corp_known_asns) and bytes > 1GB

objectives.title: DNS-tunnelling search
objectives.falsification_criterion: If DNS query-length and txt-record distributions show no entropy / volume anomalies per source, DNS-tunnelled exfil is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | summarize avg(query_length), p99(query_length), count() by client_ip | where p99 > 200 and count() > 1000

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, smb; impact: data-breach, fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, Active Directory.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW
article.summary: View CSAF Summary RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW contains multiple vulnerabilities that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary SQL commands on the underlying database, retrieve sensitive administrative credentials, escalate privileges, and perform unauthorized operations such as modifying system configurations or causing a denial of service. Siemens has released a new version for RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW and recommends to update to the latest version. The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW are affected: RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW vers:intdot/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW 4 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection'), Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key, Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data, Client-Side Enforcement of Server-Side Security Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-89196 Affected devices do not properly validate or sanitize input in facility names processed during the Bulk Import/Export workflow. This could allow an authenticated attacker with specific privileges to execute arbitrary SQL commands on the underlying database. Read More 1 Affected Product RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Product Status: known_affected Remedia

General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-89196, CVE-2026-89197, CVE-2026-89198; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; impact: ddos.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Kiloview E3 NDI Encoder
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to fully compromise the device. The following versions of Kiloview E3 NDI Encoder are affected: E3 Firmware CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.9 Kiloview E3 Firmware 6 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection'), Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Insufficient Session Expiration, Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal'), NULL Pointer Dereference, Use of Hard-coded Credentials Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Communications, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: China Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-109122 The network management service on affected Kiloview E3 NDI encoder firmware fails to sanitize one field used when configuring static routes via the web management API. An authenticated web user with permission to configure static routes can exploit this to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root, and the malicious configuration persists across reboots. Successful exploitation could result in full device compromise, including exposure of stored credentials and cryptographic material. these vulnerabilities to CISA. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-109122 affecting the affected product/service
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-109122 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-109122, CVE-2026-111100, CVE-2026-96616; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-109122.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-109122 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-109122/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-109122 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-109122')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-109122, CVE-2026-111100, CVE-2026-96616; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.kiloview.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.

objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

article.title: Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI, IoTWorX, MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code (CVE-2023-4863), bypass authentication (CVE-2026-16436 and CVE-2026-16437), or perform arbitrary operations (CVE-2026-16438), resulting in information disclosure, tampering with, destruction, or deletion of information, and a denial-of-service (DoS) condition of the system. article.raw_text: Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI, IoTWorX, MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code (CVE-2023-4863), bypass authentication (CVE-2026-16436 and CVE-2026-16437), or perform arbitrary operations (CVE-2026-16438), resulting in information disclosure, tampering with, destruction, or deletion of information, and a denial-of-service (DoS) condition of the system. The following versions of Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI, IoTWorX, MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz are affected: Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS64 >=10.97| Mitsubishi Electric ICONICS Suite >=10.97| Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS64 Mitsubishi Electric ICONICS Suite Mitsubishi Electric Hyper Historian Mitsubishi Electric AnalytiX Mitsubishi Electric MobileHMI Mitsubishi Electric IoTWorX Mitsubishi Electric MC Works64 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-16436, CVE-2026-16437, CVE-2026-16438) Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS32 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-16436, CVE-2026-16437) Mitsubishi Electric BizViz vers:all/* (CVE-2026-16436, CVE-2026-16437) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.1 Mitsubishi Electric Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS64 3 Vulnerabilities Out-of-bounds Write, Weak Password Recovery Mechanism for Forgotten Password, Incorrect Privilege Assignment Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2023-4863 Out-of-bounds Write (CWE-787) vulnerability caused by libwebp, an internal component in GENESIS64 and ICONICS Suite could allow an authenticated local attacker to cause a heap-based buffer overflow and execute arbitrary code by importing a crafted file as an administrator for the affected product. As a result, the attacker may disclose internal information, tamper with, destroy, or delete internal information, or cause the affected system to enter a denial-of-service (DoS) condition. Read More 4 Affected Products Mitsubishi Electric GENESIS64: >=10.97| Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Mitsubishi Electric is releasing fixed version 10.97.3 or later for GENESIS64 and ICONICS Suite. Please download the fixed version from the link below and install it: "https://iconicsinc.my.site.com/community/s/resource-center/product-downloads". (Note: GENESIS64 is included in the ICONICS Suite installation.) For more information on the fixed version, please refer to the Mitsubishi Electric security advisory at "https://www.mitsubishielectric.com/psirt/vulnerability/pdf/2026-006_en.pdf". Mitigation For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend configuring the PCs with the affected product installed so that only an administrator can log in, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. Mitigation For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend using the PCs with the affected product installed in the LAN and blocking remote login from untrusted networks and hosts, and from non-administrator users, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. Mitigation For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend blocking unauthorized access by using a firewall, virtual private network (VPN), etc. and allowing remote login only to administrator when internet access is required, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. Mitigation For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend restricting physical access to the PC with the affected product installed and the network to which the PC is connected, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. Mitigation For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend preventing the user from clicking on web links in emails from untrusted sources, or from opening attachments in untrusted emails, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. Mitigation For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend installing anti-virus software on the PC with the affected product installed, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2023-4863 affecting the affected product/service
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2023-4863 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2023-4863, CVE-2026-16436, CVE-2026-16437; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2023-4863.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2023-4863 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2023-4863/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2023-4863 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2023-4863')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2023-4863, CVE-2026-16436, CVE-2026-16437; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('iconicsinc.my.site.com','www.mitsubishielectric.com','iconics.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2023-4863, CVE-2026-16436, CVE-2026-16437; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: A quiet week in infosec <.<
article.summary: In this edition of the Threat Source newsletter, William explores how PHP has taken over the conversation, Node.js has joined in, but underneath it all, there are still good people doing good work.
article.raw_text: A quiet week in infosec <.< In this edition of the Threat Source newsletter, William explores how PHP has taken over the conversation, Node.js has joined in, but underneath it all, there are still good people doing good work. Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter. “The darkest period of my life, so far, arrived the summer I was pregnant with my eldest son. The future was growing in me with all of its terrifying unpredictability, and I found myself anxious, unable to work and woefully at sea.” — Lauren Groff I doubt Lauren had this maniacal infosec news cycle in mind when she wrote about the terrifyingly unpredictable future, but honestly, she’s got our current careers down cold. Let he who is not woefully at sea cast the first water balloon? I’ll work on it. Here we are with PHP taking up every available ounce of oxygen, Node.js adding its own spice to the sauce... and here’s me, staring my screen blankly, waiting for an original thought to leak out and onto this page. Not to worry, none have. There is simply nothing novel to say because the entire internet has it covered. In triplicate. With graphs and compelling statistics and AI-generated evil bad guy images galore. These vulnerabilities are serious, and the remediations matter. Teams need to know what they run, find the affected systems, and get them patched and determine ways to secure systems that can’t be patched. I’m simply not going to add another dramatic headline to the stack or pretend there’s a clever new angle hiding in the margins. The thing I keep looping on is that the work underneath the headlines is familiar and it’s the real story. To defend your environment, you need a team that knows that environment, has enough time and expertise to investigate the telemetry, that can tell an anomaly from the usual benign noise, and take action. Yes, the right tools help, and without them you can’t do it — but the people doing the work are still what make those tools useful. Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. This is the entire ballgame. Read it again: Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. Because a good response starts way before the headline. Know what you own, who owns it, what version is running, whether it can be reached from the internet, what identities can do what task on the device, etc. When a fix is available, make sure it actually reaches the system you meant to fix. If a system cannot be updated yet, give that exception an owner and a deadline. Reduce its exposure, add monitoring, and keep checking until the fix is in place. “We’ll get to it” is not a plan. So, there may be nothing new to say about PHP this week, but the work is still worth talking about: Know your environment, take care of your team members, and keep paying attention when the weird thing stops being weird and starts becoming evidence. When the next headline arrives, help your teammate do the same. “The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next.” — Ursula K. Le Guin The one big thing Cisco Talos has recently discovered "NIK C2," a new command-and-control framework that integrates AI directly into its attack chain. This Go-based Windows implant allows adversaries to dump credentials, stream keystrokes, and deploy screen-locking ransomware. It also uses an integrated OpenAI model to analyze harvested data on the fly. By hijacking the victim's own API keys to fund these requests, NIK C2 collapses data collection and exploitation into a single, continuous session. Why do I care? By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, NIK C2 turns a compromised host into an active operational asset rather than a passive foothold. Because it processes data and generates context-aware payloads locally, it erases the offline processing delays that historically gave defenders a critical detection window. Furthermore, by piggybacking on the victim's OpenAI account, threat actors completely mask their infrastructure, leaving no attributable trace and complicating incident response. So now what? Defenders must embrace continuous behavioral vigilance. Ensure endpoint solutions monitor for unusual local proxy routing, unexpected PowerShell executions, and unauthorized access to browser databases or crypto wallets. Update your defenses using the ClamAV signature and indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided in the full blog . Top security headlines of the week CISA gives agencies days to patch critical PHP bugs CISA added the two vulnerabilities in the PHP open-source scripting software to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog Monday. ( Federal News Network ) Node2Shell: Brotli flaw triggers patching across Microsoft, Node.js, Python packages An out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder affects Node.js, .NET, PowerShell, and Python packages, and can lead to code execution. ( SecurityWeek ) Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens to steal private repository secrets via Actions logs Each workflow sits on a new branch named ci-sync- followed by six random characters. Deleting a branch, or the run it started, does not undo the exposure. ( The Hacker News ) Japan internet giant GMO says hackers posted stolen customer data GMO Internet is investigating a data leak after suspected unauthorized access to its Onamae cloud desktop service, which provides virtualized desktops to financial traders. ( TechCrunch ) Third Serengeti sweep tops 1,400 arrests as investigations mature Interpol's annual Operation Serengeti, now on its third iteration, led to 1,462 arrests across 20 African countries and the U.S., recovering $105 million in stolen funds. ( Dark Reading ) Can’t get enough Talos? Stealing AI secrets and breaking EDRs Phishing may have dropped from last quarter's highs, but ransomware engagements climbed as attackers shifted their focus toward disabling EDR systems and scraping AI credentials. The financial sector also returned as a top target. From federal SOCs to Talos: Ryan Fetterman on practical security research What does it mean to be "blue collar" for the blue team? Amy sat down with security researcher Ryan Fetterman to discuss his journey from federal agency work to his new role at Talos. The Guy Who Invented Pain (plus first reactions to PHP2Shell) David Bianco built the Pyramid of Pain, so we offered him some more. David joins the Beers with Talos crew for a conversation how AI changes about his famous model, how EvidenceForge creates simulated incidents for research and training, and why his red-team entrance exam didn’t go to plan. Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates Cisco Talos is aware of eight compromised intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority. eMudhra has revoked the certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. Two critical RCEs in PHP core Two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP core could have implications across its wider ecosystem. This blog explains what we know so far, and details the Snort coverage available. Upcoming events where you can find Talos SAINTCON (Oct. 26 – 30) Provo, UT CYBERWARCON (Nov. 20) Arlington, VA AVAR 2026 (Dec. 2 – 4) Hyderabad, India Black Hat Europe (Dec. 7 – 10) London, U.K. Most prevalent malware files from Talos telemetry over the past week SHA256: 73a25ff8893260418c2271b863c567e40e842adbab3c57023cb72de590ea377d MD5: 0cf0271c3564881fce95f44c649bd745 Talos Rep: https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=73a25ff8893260418c2271b863c567e40e842adbab3c57023cb72de590ea377d Example Filename: KMSAuto++.exe Detection Name: HackTool:WZTeam-tpd SHA256: 9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507 MD5: 2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f Talos Rep: https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507 Example Filename: sample.exe Detection Name: W32.9F1F11A708-100.SBX.TG** SHA256: 7fc50b69b56bfdfa9fc0a3e088ff13904587d6336a51e9edcc7919cba83d4e3f MD5: cca616647db9370c88998ae25da6997f Talos Rep: https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=7fc50b69b56bfdfa9fc0a3e088ff13904587d6336a51e9edcc7919cba83d4e3f Example Filename: cca616647db9370c88998ae25da6997f.exe Detection Name: Win.Tool.Kmsauto::1201 SHA256: 58d6fec4ba24c32d38c9a0c7c39df3cb0e91f500b323e841121d703c7b718681 MD5: f1fe671bcefd4630e5ed8b87c9283534 Talos Rep: https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=58d6fec4ba24c32d38c9a0c7c39df3cb0e91f500b323e841121d703c7b718681 Example Filename: KMSAuto Net.exe Detection Name: W32.58D6FEC4BA-95.SBX.TG SHA256: fed979f93bcaf4e73ebd25748093a92095d5109cbd01d55f97bdc50ce509ad2f MD5: 207d9d891ac756b2bfad88aba5682c65 Talos Rep: https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=fed979f93bcaf4e73ebd25748093a92095d5109cbd01d55f97bdc50ce509ad2f Example Filename: sample.exe Detection Name: W32.FED979F93B-95.SBX.TG

objectives.title: Anomalous remote logons (Type 3 / Type 10)
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4624 logon-type 3/10 events show no bursts from a single source to many destinations, lateral movement via RDP/SMB is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id in (4624) and logon_type in (3,10) | summarize dests = dcount(dst_host) by src_user, src_host | where dests > 10

objectives.title: Admin-tool usage outside baseline
objectives.falsification_criterion: If PsExec / WMIC / PowerShell remoting / Impacket-style usage is absent outside known admin jump-hosts, the lateral-tool hypothesis is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('psexec.exe','psexesvc.exe','wmic.exe','wsmprovhost.exe') and host !in (admin_jumphosts)

objectives.title: Kerberos abuse telemetry
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4769 ticket requests show no anomalous RC4 / odd-SPN patterns and no AS-REP roasting indicators, credential-based lateral movement is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id == 4769 and ticket_encryption == 'RC4-HMAC' | summarize by target_spn, account_name

objectives.title: Lateral file-copy staging
objectives.falsification_criterion: If SMB writes of archives / executables across multiple hosts from one user/host are absent, lateral staging is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: file | where action == 'write' and ext in ('.7z','.rar','.zip','.exe') and dest matches /\\\\.*\\(C\$|admin\$)/

hypotheses.title: Data staging and exfiltration to attacker-controlled storage
hypotheses.statement: Sensitive data has been staged (archived) and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled endpoints or cloud-storage tenants in the reporting window.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'exfiltration' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit; impact: ransomware, data-breach, fraud; products: Microsoft Exchange.

objectives.title: Cloud-storage exfil to non-corp tenants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If DLP / proxy show no uploads to mega.nz, anonfiles, transfer.sh, or personal Dropbox/OneDrive tenants, cloud exfil is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: proxy | where host matches /mega\.nz|anonfiles\.com|transfer\.sh|filebin\.net/ | summarize bytes = sum(bytes_out) by user

objectives.title: Archive-then-egress pattern
objectives.falsification_criterion: If user/host telemetry shows no archive creation (rar/7z) within minutes of a large outbound transfer, the stage-then-exfil pattern is absent.
objectives.suggested_query: file_create | where ext in ('.rar','.7z','.zip') | join (egress | where bytes_out > 50MB) on host within 30m

objectives.title: Outbound volume to rare ASNs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If outbound bytes-by-ASN over the last 30 days show no first-seen / low-reputation destination receiving >1GB, bulk exfil is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: netflow | summarize bytes = sum(bytes_out) by asn | where asn !in (corp_known_asns) and bytes > 1GB

objectives.title: DNS-tunnelling search
objectives.falsification_criterion: If DNS query-length and txt-record distributions show no entropy / volume anomalies per source, DNS-tunnelled exfil is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | summarize avg(query_length), p99(query_length), count() by client_ip | where p99 > 200 and count() > 1000

article.title: Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller
article.summary: View CSAF Summary RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) contains multiple vulnerabilities in the integrated SQLite component that could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code, cause a denial of service, or obtain sensitive information. Siemens has released a new version for RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) and recommends to update to the latest version. The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller are affected: RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) vers:intdot/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.8 Siemens RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW Station Access Controller (SAC) 4 Vulnerabilities Numeric Truncation Error, Improper Clearing of Heap Memory Before Release ('Heap Inspection'), Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding, Heap-based Buffer Overflow Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2025-6965 There exists a vulnerability in SQLite versions before 3.50.2 where the number of aggregate terms could exceed the number of columns available. This could lead to a memory corruption issue. We recommend upgrading to version 3.50.2 or above.
