article.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks a fake-download campaign that uses trojanized Inno installers to deliver multiple monetization offers and provides detection and investigation guidance across the complete installer session. The post Fake-download campaign uses trojanized installers to deliver monetization payloads appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .
article.raw_text: Fake-download campaign uses trojanized installers to deliver monetization payloads Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks a fake-download campaign that uses trojanized Inno installers to deliver multiple monetization offers and provides detection and investigation guidance across the complete installer session. The post Fake-download campaign uses trojanized installers to deliver monetization payloads appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog . In this article Attack chain overview Mitigation and protection guidance Learn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session. Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks. Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms. This blog details the campaign’s execution model and confirmed outcomes and provides mitigation guidance, Microsoft Defender protection information, advanced hunting queries, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and indicators of compromise to help defenders identify, investigate, and respond to related activity. Attack chain overview The fake-download campaign follows a four-stage attack chain that progresses from deceptive lures through Inno-based staging, offer-controlled payload delivery, and installation of one or more monetization branches: Initial access via fake download lures – Users run fake installers promoted as cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, executors, or unofficial utilities. Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging – The installer launches an Inno Setup-style temporary runner under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ , which starts recurring eld*.exe , set_*.exe , or other numbered stages. Offer execution callback and payload delivery – The runner contacts rotating infrastructure using a repeatable d=inno and r=offer_execution callback pattern. Offer, affiliate, download-network, placement, and session values coordinate downstream payload selection and correlate activity within the installer session. Final payload installation and monetization – Staged payloads use unattended installation switches to install one or more confirmed campaign branches: WorldProxyPool for proxy and network-resource monetization; CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC) for compute-resource monetization; or Advanced Windows (AW) Manager and Windows Manager for adware-style utility monetization. WorldProxyPool also creates recurring SYSTEM scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updater activity. Attack Chain Figure 1. Overview of the attack chain. Initial access via fake download lures The campaign begins when users download and run fake installers promoted as cracked software, game installers, executors, activators, plugins, utilities, or driver and mobile-unlock tools. Observed lures include cracked audio plugins, PC games, Roblox executors, auto-clickers, driver tools, and fake utility installers. Example lures: Echo Client; FabFilter Total Bundle; Navicat Premium crack; Cue Club; auto-clicker; Deadpool Apunka Games; Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2; TFT Unlock Tool; and clownfishvoicechanger. Figure 2. Example utility download lure. Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging Across the investigated activity, user-launched lures spawned Inno Setup-style temporary runners under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ and then launched one or more numbered eld*.exe stages. Arguments such as /SL5 , /SPAWNWND , and /FIRSTWND , together with the temporary path and numbered stage names, provide more durable indicators than the original lure filename. The depth of the execution chain and its downstream outcome varied by installer session. One Echo Client example progressed through multiple numbered stages and reached several monetization branches, while other observed lures exposed fewer numbered stages or downstream components. The table below uses the Echo Client activity as a representative example of the wrapper-to-stage sequence; individual installer sessions may launch different combinations of numbered stages. Step Process Command-line / path signal Role 1 Echo Client.exe Launched from %USERPROFILE%\Downloads\Echo Client\ User-launched lure 2 Echo Client.tmp %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\… with /SL5=… Inno temporary runner 3 Echo Client.exe /SPAWNWND=… /FIRSTWND=… Inno child process / window handoff 4 Echo Client.tmp /SL5=… /SPAWNWND=… /FIRSTWND=… Temporary runner continues execution 5 eld*.exe eld0.exe , eld1.exe , eld3.exe , eld4.exe , and eld5.exe under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ Numbered staged payloads Table 1. Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging. Offer execution callback and payload delivery After staging, the Inno temporary runner contacted rotating callback infrastructure using randomized URL paths but a repeatable query-string structure: http:// / ?sis= &fz= &d=inno&r=offer_execution&ko=no&o= &a= &dn= &spot= &t= &cr= Failed or blocked offers used r=offer_execution_fail and sometimes included local error text, including messages that the operation did not complete because the file contained a virus or potentially unwanted software. These callbacks are useful campaign-attribution and sequencing markers, but they are not always the earliest prevention point. In some endpoint detection and response (EDR) traces, child payloads launched before or around the r=offer_execution callback. The campaign used offer IDs, affiliate IDs, download-network IDs, and placement values to select or report downstream payload attempts. Observed offer and download-network combinations included o=1712 / dn=507 , o=1720 / dn=536 , o=1727 / dn=564 , o=1729 / dn=566 , o=331 / dn=244 , o=1674 / dn=440 , o=1675 / dn=441 , o=1681 / dn=447 , and o=1730 / dn=567 . Different offers could succeed or fail independently within the same installer session, so a failed first offer did not necessarily mean that the full bundle stopped. Parameter Observed use Assessment d Often set to inno Installer or delivery-family marker sis Stable within an installer session Session-correlation value a Stable across related requests Affiliate, campaign, or distribution-partner identifier o Changes by offer Offer identifier dn / on Changes with the offer or retrieval path Download-network or offer-network field; exact meaning unconfirmed spot Increments through the session Offer placement, slot, or execution order paw Present across offer requests Request, package, or session-correlation value; exact meaning unconfirmed fz Present in outcome callbacks Delivered package size or file-size field t Present in outcome callbacks Timing, token, or request value; exact meaning unconfirmed r offer_execution or offer_execution_fail Per-offer execution result msg Present on failed offers Error text from the local download or installation attempt ko / cr Boolean-like or short values Server-side control or result flags; exact meaning unconfirmed Table 2. Assessments are based on observed telemetry correlations, not confirmed server-side definitions. Offer / download-network pair Semantic meaning o=1712 / dn=507 Primary first-stage offer commonly attempted at the start of the installer flow. o=1720 / dn=536 Offer branch associated with CharityEngine/BOINC distributed-compute monetization. o=1727 / dn=564 Offer branch associated with WorldProxyPool proxyware monetization. o=1729 / dn=566 Recurring follow-on offer branch in the installer flow. o=331 / dn=244 Secondary offer branch observed in the multi-offer sequence. o=1674 / dn=440 Later campaign offer branch. o=1675 / dn=441 Low-volume offer branch. o=1681 / dn=447 Additional offer branch in the campaign’s installer rotation. o=1730 / dn=567 Later high-volume offer branch. Table 3. Offer and download-network pairs and their semantic roles in the installer flow. The campaign rotated callback domains frequently while preserving the same d=inno and offer-execution callback structure across recurring lure categories. Individual domains are therefore short-lived infrastructure indicators; the durable hunting signal is the combination of the callback pattern, Inno temporary execution, staged filenames, and related installer-session activity. The full observed domain set is provided in the IOC section. Final payload installation and monetization After offer callback and payload delivery, the campaign launched downstream installers or components using unattended installation switches such as /qn , /S , /quiet , and /norestart . This stage converted the fake-download execution chain into installed software and recurring execution across three monetization branches: proxy and network-resource monetization, compute-resource monetization, and adware-style utility monetization. Branch Primary behavior Representative artifacts A. WorldProxyPool Proxy agent installation and scheduled-task setup sdk-agent.exe; sdk-agent.updater.exe; watchdog.ps1; WorldProxyPoolAgent task B. CharityEngine / BOINC Distributed-compute software installation boinc.exe; charityengine.exe; ce11.exe; VirtualBox-7.2.8-r173730.msi C. AW Manager / Windows Manager Utility and updater-style software installation Windows Manager – Postback Johan.msi; AdvancedWindowsManager.exe; Windows Updater.exe Table 4. Summary of the three monetization branches and representative artifacts. Proxy and network-resource monetization — WorldProxyPool In the WorldProxyPool branch, a staged eld4.exe payload created three SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for components under C:\Program Files\WorldProxyPool\ . WorldProxyPoolAgent configured sdk-agent.exe to run at system startup with highest privileges; WorldProxyPoolWatchdog configured a hidden, noninteractive PowerShell watchdog script to run every five minutes; and WorldProxyPoolUpdater configured sdk-agent.updater.exe update to run hourly. The installer also started the agent task immediately with schtasks.exe /Run . Subsequent task launches were brokered by the Windows Task Scheduler service ( svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule ), causing sdk-agent.exe and the watchdog script to execute in the service context. This persistence mechanism supports recurring proxy-agent, watchdog, and updater activity, consistent with network-resource monetization. Scheduled task Purpose WorldProxyPoolAgent Runs sdk-agent.exe at system startup as SYSTEM with highest privileges; the installer also started it immediately with schtasks.exe /Run . WorldProxyPoolWatchdog Runs a hidden, noninteractive PowerShell watchdog script every five minutes as SYSTEM with highest privileges. WorldProxyPoolUpdater Runs sdk-agent.updater.exe update hourly as SYSTEM with highest privileges. Table 5. WorldProxyPool scheduled tasks created during the proxyware installation chain Figure 3. WorldProxyPool installation and persistence. eld4.exe created SYSTEM-level startup, five-minute watchdog, and hourly updater tasks. Compute-resource monetization — CharityEngine and BOINC In the CharityEngine and BOINC branch, the offer payload installed distributed-compute software and supporting components under C:\Program Files\BOINC\ and C:\ProgramData\BOINC\ . Observed components included ce-installer_7.14.2_vbox-7.2.8.exe , ce_7.14.2_windows_x86_64.exe , charityengine.exe , boinc.exe , boinctray.exe , boinc.scr , boincscr.exe , wrapper_2022110901_windows_x86_64.exe , ce11.exe , and VirtualBox-7.2.8-r173730.msi . They covered BOINC launch, compute-wrapper execution, GPU or compute-capability checks, CharityEngine project communication, and VirtualBox installation. Figure 4. CharityEngine/BOINC compute-monetization branch. Adware-style utility monetization: AdvancedWindowsManager / Windows Manager The same Inno offer-execution infrastructure delivered an AW Manager or Windows Manager branch. In one observed process tree, the Inno runner spawned eld3.exe , launched Windows Manager – Postback Johan.msi , and installed AdvancedWindowsManager.exe and Windows Updater.exe under paths resembling %APPDATA%\AW Manager\Windows Manager 1.0.0\ or C:\Program Files (x86)\AW Manager\Windows Manager\ . Figure 5. AW Manager / Windows Manager utility-install branch. Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft recommends the following actions to reduce exposure to this campaign and detect related activity: Preventive controls Avoid untrusted software sources. Do not download cracked software, key generators, unofficial game installers, or software activation tools, which are common delivery mechanisms for malware, potentially unwanted applications, and monetization campaigns. Enable cloud-delivered protection. Verify that Microsoft Defender Antivirus cloud-delivered protection is enabled to improve detection of emerging malware and potentially unwanted applications. See: Configure cloud-delivered protection Keep tamper protection enabled. Use tamper protection to help prevent unauthorized changes to Microsoft Defender security settings. See: Learn about tamper protection . Enable reputation-based protection. Configure reputation-based protection to help block known malicious and untrusted applications and downloads. See: Configure reputation-based protection . Consider Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) protections. Evaluate ASR rules, including rules that block executable files unless they meet prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria. See: Review Attack Surface Reduction rules . Investigation actions Investigate execution from Inno temporary directories. Review activity from paths such as %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ , particularly when staged executables such as eld*.exe , set_*.exe , FirstFast[1].exe , or SecondRunner[1].exe are observed. Correlate Inno callback activity. Monitor outbound requests containing d=inno together with r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail, and review related process, file, and network activity across the complete installer session. Review unexpected scheduled tasks. Investigate newly created scheduled tasks, particularly tasks running with SYSTEM privileges or recurring watchdog and updater functions. See: Audit scheduled task creation events . Audit software inventory for unexpected installations. Review endpoints for the presence of software such as WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, VirtualBox, or other applications that users did not intentionally install. See: Review software inventory in Defender Vulnerability Management . Microsoft Defender XDR detections Microsoft Defender detects and blocks campaign-linked payloads through cloud protection, machine-learning classifications, network inspection, and behavior monitoring. Relevant observed detections include remote-thread injection, scheduled-task launch, and suspicious outbound HTTP activity. Customers with provisioned access can also use Microsoft Security Copilot in Microsoft Defender to investigate and respond to incidents, hunt for threats, and protect their organization with relevant threat intelligence. Tactic Observed activity Microsoft Defender coverage Initial access and execution Users execute fake cracked-software installers, including files presented as Navicat Premium or FabFilter bundles, from Downloads, archive-extraction folders, or Inno extraction paths. The installers launch temporary payloads from %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\. Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DA!MTB – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DB!MTB Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – A suspicious file was observed – An active ‘Wacatac’ malware was detected – ‘Kepavll’ malware was prevented Command and control / campaign tracking Outbound callbacks use a stable Inno offer-execution URL contract: d=inno with r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail . Each callback reports an individual offer result. Correlating these callbacks with process, file, network, persistence, and installation events provides visibility across the multi-offer session. Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Behavior:Win32/SuspInnoOffer.A!mapsi Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Suspicious ‘SuspInnoOffer’ behavior was blocked Staging and payload delivery The installer chain drops multiple staged files from Inno temporary directories, commonly named eld*.exe , set_*.exe , FirstFast[1].exe , and SecondRunner[1].exe . Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DA!MTB – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DB!MTB Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – A suspicious file was observed – An active ‘Wacatac’ malware was detected – An active ‘Egairtigado’ malware was blocked – ‘Kepavll’ malware was prevented Persistence In the investigated Navicat chain, WorldProxyPool created SYSTEM scheduled tasks with highest privileges: WorldProxyPoolAgent at startup, WorldProxyPoolWatchdog every five minutes through hidden noninteractive PowerShell, and WorldProxyPoolUpdater hourly. It also wrote uninstall metadata under the WorldProxyPool registry key. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Suspicious scheduled task activity – Suspicious Scheduled Task Process Launched – Suspicious Task Scheduler activity Resource hijacking / monetization Two monetization paths were confirmed. The Navicat chain installed WorldProxyPool proxyware. The FabFilter chain silently installed CharityEngine/BOINC, VirtualBox, and Visual C++ components, launched BOINC workloads, and contacted CharityEngine infrastructure. Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Adware:Win32/Clover – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DA!MTB – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DB!MTB Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – An active ‘Clover’ malware was detected – An active ‘Wacatac’ malware was detected Defense evasion and suspicious behavior Several staged payloads are associated with defense-evasion, execution, persistence, remote-thread, and other suspicious behaviors. Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Trojan:Win32/OffLoader.A Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Suspicious ‘SuspEtherRpcConn’ behavior was blocked – Suspicious ‘SuspSmsScanConn’ behavior was blocked Microsoft Security Copilot Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run prebuilt promptbooks to automate investigation and response tasks related to this campaign. Useful promptbooks include: Incident investigation Microsoft User analysis Threat actor profile Threat Intelligence 360 report based on MDTI intelligence Vulnerability impact assessment. Some promptbooks require access to Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Sentinel, or related Microsoft security plugins. For this campaign, analysts can prompt Security Copilot to summarize and correlate available incident evidence, subject to connected data and permissions. Threat intelligence reports Microsoft customers can use Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics and related Microsoft threat intelligence reporting to track this rotating, multi-offer fake-download campaign and review updates on its Inno callbacks, offer outcomes, staged payloads, infrastructure, and proxyware or distributed-compute results. The reporting helps analysts correlate offer callbacks and endpoint activity from the same installer session, identify devices with associated monetization stages, and assess the overall bundle outcome. It also provides investigation context, protection guidance, relevant indicators, and recommended response actions. Advanced hunting Microsoft Defender XDR customers can run the following advanced hunting queries to find related activity in their networks. Inno offer-execution callbacks DeviceNetworkEvents | where RemoteUrl has "d=inno" | where RemoteUrl has_any ("r=offer_execution", "r=offer_execution_fail") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName Payload execution from Inno temporary directories DeviceProcessEvents | where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\is-" | where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^(eld[0-9]+|set_[0-9]+|FirstFast(?:\[1\])?|SecondRunner(?:\[1\])?)\.exe$" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256 Outbound connections to observed campaign infrastructure DeviceNetworkEvents | where RemoteUrl has_any ("orbittrack.cfd", "prairielink.cfd", "willowbox.xyz", "stonestation.cfd", "foldlodge.xyz", "friendsanchor.xyz", "fallport.cfd", "wishcourt.cfd", "cratebase.cfd", "belieftrack.cfd", "beliefdesk.xyz", "companyharbor.xyz", "signalpane.cfd", "inkact.xyz", "wishgrove.cfd") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName Hunting note: Treat each callback as an individual offer result. Group events by device, time window, and available session or affiliate fields, then correlate the callbacks with Inno temporary execution, staged filenames, scheduled-task creation, and monetization-software activity. Domain-only matches are leads, not confirmation. Validate the queries against the current Microsoft Defender XDR schema before publication. MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed The following MITRE ATT&CK mappings reflect behaviors observed in the investigated activity. Mappings are limited to evidence described in this report. Execution T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File | A user launches an installer presented as cracked software, a game, an activator, a plugin, or an unofficial utility. Persistence T1053.005 Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task | WorldProxyPool creates SYSTEM-level startup, watchdog, and updater tasks; the watchdog runs every five minutes and the updater runs hourly. Defense evasion T1036 Masquerading | Installers are presented with names and branding associated with cracked commercial software or unofficial software bundles to encourage execution. T1564.003 Hide Artifacts: Hidden Window | The WorldProxyPool watchdog invokes PowerShell with hidden, noninteractive execution options. Command and control T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols | The installer sends HTTP callbacks to rotating infrastructure using the durable d=inno and r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail query pattern. T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer | The campaign retrieves staged executables and supporting components from threat actor-controlled, cloud-storage, and content delivery network (CDN)-hosted locations. Impact T1496 Resource Hijacking | The campaign installs CharityEngine/BOINC for distributed computing and WorldProxyPool for proxyware monetization, abusing victim compute and network resources through deceptive bundled installation. For standard industry documentation about these techniques, refer to the MITRE ATT&CK framework . Indicators of compromise (IOC) The following indicators of compromise (IOCs) were observed during investigation of this campaign and can assist defenders in identifying related activity and conducting threat-hunting efforts. C:\Program Files\WorldProxyPool\sdk-agent.exe File path WorldProxyPool proxyware component. hypotheses.title: Initial access via the disclosed vulnerability affecting Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting the disclosed vulnerability in Microsoft 365 / Entra ID within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit; impact: fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for the referenced CVE.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Microsoft 365 / Entra ID' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for the referenced CVE in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-the referenced CVE/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the the referenced CVE fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('the referenced CVE')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Microsoft 365 / Entra ID hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit; impact: fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('client.exe','client.tmp','eld0.exe') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit; impact: fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks
article.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzes the LiteLLM 1.107.0 compromise, including Python startup hooks, credential theft, remote code loading, detections, and mitigations. The post Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .
article.raw_text: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzes the LiteLLM 1.107.0 compromise, including Python startup hooks, credential theft, remote code loading, detections, and mitigations. The post Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog . In this article Attack overview Technical details Mitigation and protection guidance Indicators of compromise References Learn More On October 21, 2026, a compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release was published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) and distributed through official container images. The malicious package added files that Python could execute during normal interpreter initialization. An application did not need to import LiteLLM for the payload to run: starting Python in an affected environment could be enough. Microsoft analyzed two execution paths in the affected wheels: a credential collector launched through a path extension, and a Unix-oriented loader persisted through site-specific configuration. The collector targeted authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. A separate database module attempted to read selected credential and model-configuration records from the LiteLLM proxy. Endpoint observations on Windows and macOS matched the recovered collector’s discovery, encryption, and outbound-connection behavior. In one Windows example, a routine Python invocation to install an unrelated dependency activated the collector. This distinction matters for response: investigators should not start Python or pip inside a suspect environment to determine whether the malicious package is present. This blog explains the startup mechanisms, the credentials the payload could reach, and the evidence defenders can use to investigate exposure. It also provides Microsoft Defender detection information, advanced hunting queries, and recovery guidance. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery. Organizations must address the affected Python environment, any surviving processes, and credentials accessible to the compromised identity. Attack overview LiteLLM is commonly deployed as a gateway between applications and model providers. In that position it may have access to model-provider API keys, database connection strings, workload identities, routing configuration, and tenant policy data. The same package is also used on developer workstations, build agents, test systems, and containers, which widened the set of environments that could be exposed by the compromised release. According to LiteLLM maintainers , stolen developer GitHub credentials were used to alter the release workflow and redirect it to the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm rather than the legitimate BerriAI/litellm repository. A credential associated with another developer account was then used to satisfy a production approval step. Microsoft has not independently determined how the attacker first accessed the upstream environment or obtained those credentials. The compromised package used Python startup mechanisms to execute malicious code automatically, meaning exposure was not limited to systems actively using a LiteLLM gateway. Developer workstations, continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment (CI/CD) agents, test environments, containers, and other systems that started Python with the affected package installed could also execute the payload. The malicious code supported credential collection and, on Unix-based systems, retrieval and execution of additional Python code. Figure 1: Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 execution flow. 1. Compromised package distribution The compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release delivered malicious Python startup files to environments where the package was installed. 2. Automatic payload execution Python startup processing launched the credential collector without requiring the application to actively use LiteLLM gateway functionality. 3. Credential and sensitive-data collection The collector targeted developer credentials, cloud credentials, browser data, SSH material, environment variables, and LiteLLM database data accessible to the affected process. 4. Encryption and exfiltration Collected data was encrypted and transmitted to an attacker-controlled endpoint. 5. Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code On Unix-based systems, the payload supported retrieving and executing additional Python code, although this activity was not confirmed. Technical details Compromised package distribution and automatic payload execution The compromised wheel packaged cook.pth , cook.py , and sitecustomize.py under litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/ . During installation, these files were relocated into the Python environment’s library directory, outside the normal litellm application directory. This placement enabled execution through Python’s normal site initialization, which processes executable import statements in .pth files and later attempts to import the sitecustomize module. The first execution path began with the single executable line in cook.pth : “import cook”. This loaded cook.py , whose wrapper Base64-decoded and zlib-decompressed an embedded Python program before executing the recovered source. The program identified itself as PRIVCOLLECT and performed credential collection in a daemon thread. Figure 2. The executable .pth line imports cook, and the recovered collector starts a daemon thread after checking its inherited environment flag. Before starting the thread, the collector checked the inherited PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE environment variable. A nonempty value caused it to return; otherwise, it set the flag, limiting duplicate collection in descendant processes. After an upload returned HTTP 200, it attempted to write /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb . These duplicate-suppression gates were not containment controls: startup alone did not prove collection or upload completed, because a short-lived process could exit before the thread finished, while write failures or temporary-storage changes could leave the marker absent. Figure 3. Encode Cook.py file and decoded PRIVCOLLECT credential Stealer configuration . A second startup mechanism used sitecustomize.py , providing a separate Unix-oriented execution path with an embedded collector and functionality to retrieve and execute additional Python code from a remote host. Remote retrieval and execution through this path were not confirmed. Together, these mechanisms extended potential exposure beyond active LiteLLM deployments: simply starting Python in an affected environment could activate the malicious code, even when LiteLLM itself was never imported. Because the startup files resided outside the litellm application directory, removing only the application files could leave the malicious startup components behind. Credential and sensitive-data collection The recovered collector was designed to gather sensitive authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. It runs multiple collection modules sequentially with independent error handling, allowing collection to continue even when individual targets are unavailable or inaccessible. Target Recovered collection behavior Developer and AI tools Reads selected authentication and configuration files for AI assistants, integrated development environments (IDEs) , GitHub Copilot, VS Code, and MCP integrations. Collects fixed paths and top-level JSON files in selected tool directories under a collection budget. Source control and package ecosystems Searches Git credentials, package-manager configuration, selected dotenv files, and private-key extensions. Shallow directory walks and file-size limits constrain these searches. Cloud and workload credentials Reads AWS, Azure CLI, and Google Cloud configuration or credential caches; Kubernetes service-account files; Docker configuration; and mounted secrets. It also attempts AWS and GCP metadata credential retrieval. Browsers and user histories Accesses Chromium-family and Firefox credential-related data and browsing history, plus shell, database-client, and interactive-tool histories. Password decryption is platform- and format-dependent. Process environments Collects its own environment and, on Linux, other process environments readable through procfs. This can expose secrets beyond variables explicitly configured for the LiteLLM process. Private keys and infrastructure Targets readable Secure Shell (SSH) material and selected GNU Privacy Guard (GPG), Transport Layor Security (TLS), CI/CD, Vault, and infrastructure-tool configuration. A target appearing in the code does not establish successful access. LiteLLM proxy data When its prerequisites are satisfied, starts a Python child using Prisma to read selected fields from two proxy database tables, with a 500-row limit for each query Encryption and exfiltration After collection, the payload serializes module results and host metadata as JSON. Each run generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector. AES-256-CBC encrypts the collection document; an embedded 4,096-bit RSA public key wraps the AES key using OAEP. The OpenSSL path tries SHA-256 and then SHA-1 for OAEP, and the resulting metadata records the selected digest. Figure 4. The collector generates a fresh AES key and IV, wraps the key with RSA, and packages the encrypted collection in a gzip tar archive before attempting upload. Selected code excerpts are wrapped for readability. The collector places three members in a gzip-compressed tar archive: data.bin , containing the initialization vector (IV) and encrypted collection; key.bin , containing the wrapped AES key; and hdr.json , containing plaintext envelope metadata. It then attempts an HTTP POST to hxxp://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck , using application/octet-stream , a fixed browser-like User-Agent, and a body checksum in an X-SHA256 header. The upload routine retries and treats only HTTP 200 as success. The OpenSSL backend creates temporary directories beginning with .pc_e_ , stages input and output files and removes them after use. Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code In addition to the credential collector, the compromised package contained a separate Unix-oriented loader in sitecustomize.py , designed to retrieve and execute additional Python code. When Python starts, the loader takes an exclusive lock on /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock so that only one instance runs per host and detaches into the background. Each cycle reads a GitHub-hosted domain.txt file, which acts as a mutable pointer to an attacker-controlled server. Figure 5. The remote-loader path checks the pointer and DNS before retrieving code, then compiles and executes the response without a content-signature check. If a valid server address is returned and successfully resolved, the loader is designed to request /codepy from that server, compile the returned content, and execute it as Python code within the affected environment. This gives the attacker a mechanism to change the second-stage payload without publishing another compromised LiteLLM package. This loader is separate from the credential collector delivered directly in the compromised package. At the time the cited researchers examined domain.txt, it was empty and no second-stage retrieval or execution was confirmed. Because the file could be changed, the loader remained a re-armable remote-code execution mechanism. Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft recommends the following actions for organizations that installed, mirrored, or built images with LiteLLM 1.107.0: Find and contain every affected copy. Identify LiteLLM 1.107.0 across installed environments, uv and pip caches, internal package mirrors, lock files, build outputs, and container images. Scope mutable container tags and the relevant exposure windows once validated and compare artifacts with the customer-ready hashes in the indicators of compromise section. For background, see secure software supply chain practices and Docker image digests. Digests are preferable to mutable tags because they identify immutable image content. Prevent Python execution and investigate from outside the environment. Isolate affected developer workstations, build agents, test systems, containers, and AI gateway hosts. Where operationally safe, stop running Python processes and prevent automation from restarting them. Do not run python, pip, or other commands that invoke the affected interpreter during evidence collection; inspect the environment with trusted tools from a known-clean system. Python normally processes site configuration, including executable import lines in .pth files, during initialization. Rebuild from verified artifacts. Confirm that cook.pth , cook.py , and sitecustomize.py were removed from the environment library path. Rebuilding is more reliable than assuming that deleting the litellm directory cleaned the top-level startup files. Rotate reachable credentials from a known-clean machine. Include model-provider keys, cloud and workload credentials, CI/CD secrets, source-control and registry tokens, SSH and GPG keys, AI coding-tool tokens, and browser sessions available to the affected identity. On proxy hosts, include stored provider credentials and DATABASE_URL. Revoke affected identity sessions rather than assuming password or key rotation immediately invalidates every active token or application session. See revoke user access in Microsoft Entra ID . Correlate before declaring compromise. Combine file hashes, Python process ancestry, .pc_e_ cryptographic staging, network destination, workload identity, and subsequent cloud or identity use. Do not use package presence or a generic filename as the sole verdict. Strengthen dependency controls. Use hash-pinned lock files, verify package and image provenance, use container digests instead of floating tags, and admit packages to internal mirrors only after review. See best practices for a secure software supply chain and dependency scanning in Azure DevOps . Restrict outbound access. Developer workstations, build agents, test systems, containers, and AI gateway hosts should not have unrestricted outbound HTTP access unless required. Route outbound traffic through managed egress controls, deny unnecessary destinations, and allowlist required services. See control outbound internet access from Azure . Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint protections. Onboard supported developer workstations, build agents, and AI gateway servers to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and enable Microsoft Defender Antivirus real-time and cloud-delivered protection where supported. See configure always-on protection and configure cloud protection . Microsoft Defender XDR detections As of October 22, 2026, the following Microsoft Defender Antivirus signatures and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint alerts were available for activity associated with the compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release. Detection names and availability may change as protection is updated. Tactic Observed activity Microsoft Defender coverage Initial Access / Execution Malicious components associated with the compromised package are detected and blocked; related suspicious script and network activity is identified across endpoints and cloud workloads. Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Trojan:PyPI/Stealer.SA – Trojan:PyPI/LiteLlmSupplyChain.A – Trojan:PyPI/LiteLlmSupplyChain.B – Backdoor:PyPI/LiteLlmSupplyChain.C Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Suspicious script launched – Suspicious network connection observed Command and Control / Credential Access Credential-like data is staged by Python and followed by network activity to a public destination, including malicious-domain lookups and OpenSSL activity associated with the compromise. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Possible theft of passwords and other sensitive web browser information – Suspicious OpenSSL command launch Microsoft Defender for Cloud Microsoft Defender for Cloud triggers below detections for related activity in Azure App Service and Kubernetes workloads: – OpenSSL activity associated with possible LiteLLM compromise detected – DNS lookup of a known malicious domain Vulnerability Management Devices vulnerable to this security issue are surfaced for remediation. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management – Endpoints exposure tab in the Microsoft Defender portal: TVM-2026-0003 Threat intelligence reports Microsoft customers can use the following reports in Microsoft products to get the most up-to-date information about the threat actor, malicious activity, and techniques discussed in this blog. This report provides intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments. Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks Advanced hunting These queries support investigation of the stages discussed above. Select the appropriate lookback in Defender XDR and correlate results with environment, process and identity evidence. They are investigation leads, not standalone verdicts. Connections to the collector domain Normalize URL/hostname observations before matching the campaign domain. The query rejects suffix lookalikes such as www[.]litellm[.]dev[.]example; a match still needs process and workload context. DeviceNetworkEvents | extend UrlForParsing = iff(RemoteUrl contains "://", RemoteUrl, strcat("http://", RemoteUrl)) | extend RemoteHost = trim_end(@"\.", tolower(tostring(parse_url(UrlForParsing).Host))) | where RemoteHost in ("www.litellm.dev", "litellm.dev") | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime, ReportId Known startup-file hashes The four hashes cover LF and CRLF variants. A missing SHA-256 field limits this hunt; a generic filename is not an equivalent match. DeviceFileEvents | where SHA256 in~ ( "9dd0a3926f96a37eb86cf1ee2310d9be93139cc4ebef3ef9e2efe9531390be25", "03ac2a8b752605d1d7710979c17ff18b03dd978203ba23ba97fd8ce3d6f897ea", "34bef04fe88ac9d0aae0475630b1738681d15b94f233ac8aa46eacf5968305fa", "b6122440d0d9cb1eb1ade9933f49214da8c31288de7710c076c2680dfa528465") | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime, ReportId Inline database-collection program Look for the sensitive table/field pair together with the query API, serialization and complete output-suppression pattern. Legitimate exports may overlap. The recovered parent’s /proc prerequisite limits its applicability; raw arguments are omitted because they can contain a database secret. DeviceProcessEvents | where FileName startswith "python" or FileName startswith "platform-python" | where strlen(ProcessCommandLine) Collector-like encryption staging The staging prefix plus encryption operation identifies a behavioral lead, not an upload or a uniquely malicious OpenSSL invocation. Alternate backends are outside this query, and key-bearing arguments are not projected. DeviceProcessEvents | where FileName in~ ("openssl", "openssl.exe") | where ProcessCommandLine contains_cs ".pc_e_" | where (ProcessCommandLine contains_cs " enc " and ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "-aes-256-cbc") or ProcessCommandLine contains_cs " pkeyutl " or ProcessCommandLine contains_cs " rsautl " | extend CryptoOperation = iff( ProcessCommandLine contains_cs " enc ", "AES packaging", "RSA wrapping") | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, CryptoOperation, ProcessId, ProcessCreationTime, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime, ReportId Vulnerability/Posture Check | Is the device potentially exposed to the affected Litellm? Use this query to identify devices potentially exposed to TVM-2026-0003. A match indicates potential exposure, not confirmed exploitation or compromise. DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId == "TVM-2026-0003" CloudProcessEvents query to detect encryption before exfiltration Identifies OpenSSL public-key encryption using /tmp/.pc_ staging paths, consistent with key wrapping before potential exfiltration. CloudProcessEvents | where ProcessName == 'openssl' and ProcessCurrentWorkingDirectory has_any ('/runner/','/app','/tmp/') and ProcessCommandLine has_all ('pkeyutl','-encrypt','-pubin') and ProcessCommandLine contains '/tmp/.pc_' MITRE ATT&CK techniques observed Microsoft mapped the following techniques based on observed activity and analysis of the recovered malicious components; individual entries note where behavior was not confirmed. For standard industry documentation, refer to the MITRE ATT&CK framework . Initial Access T1195.001 Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools | Malicious files shipped in LiteLLM 1.107.0 wheels and images; upstream release abuse reported by the maintainer. Persistence T1546.018 Event Triggered Execution: Python Startup Hooks | cook.pth and sitecustomize.py run during Python site initialization. Execution T1059.006 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python | The collector runs in the interpreter; an inline Python child performs database queries. Defense Evasion T1027.013 Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File | Collector source is embedded as Base64-encoded, zlib-compressed content. T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information | cook.py decodes and decompresses the collector at runtime. Credential Access T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files | Reads authentication and configuration files for developer, AI, and cloud tools. T1552.004 Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys | Reads selected SSH, GPG, and TLS key material. T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API | Requests AWS and GCP credentials from metadata services; returned credentials were not confirmed in Microsoft telemetry. T1555.003 Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers | Copies browser databases and supports selected Chromium password recovery on Windows. Discovery T1082 System Information Discovery | systeminfo was launched by Python in an observed Windows sequence. T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery | ipconfig, route, arp, and netstat were launched by the same Python process. Collection T1005 Data from Local System | Collects selected local histories, environment variables, and configuration. Command and Control T1102.001 Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver | The loader reads its server address from a specific GitHub-hosted file. T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer | The loader can retrieve Python code from /codepy; retrieval and execution were not confirmed. Indicators of compromise URLs are defanged. Use precise roles and context rather than blocking shared infrastructure indiscriminately. Indicator Type Role www[.]litellm[.]dev Domain Exfiltration Domain hxxp://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck URL Exfiltration URL hxxps://raw[.]githubusercontent[.]com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt URL C2 dead-drop URL 9dd0a3926f96a37eb86cf1ee2310d9be93139cc4ebef3ef9e2efe9531390be25 SHA-256 cook.py, variant 03ac2a8b752605d1d7710979c17ff18b03dd978203ba23ba97fd8ce3d6f897ea SHA-256 cook.py, Windows wheel variant 34bef04fe88ac9d0aae0475630b1738681d15b94f233ac8aa46eacf5968305fa SHA-256 sitecustomize.py, variant b6122440d0d9cb1eb1ade9933f49214da8c31288de7710c076c2680dfa528465 SHA-256 sitecustomize.py, Windows wheel variant 7f191632e7320705d154b85204f1ae546b543acbd7e8861229b76f5042b92bdb SHA-256 cook.pth 84dc8c82c0a4a4a62552ef826b49fcc86d1a5c4a5d0f2c06665723f93d129d7d SHA-256 cook.pth, variant /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock file Lock file created by the background loader. /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb file Marker written after stolen data was sent. 7598727f209d717041db37f7dca271d3a7d328a279890e0e1d55375729aeb86d SHA-256 litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-macosx_10_12_x86_64.whl 0aaf7ba346d41ef2f40390436738b001180d5a1c03aa093f121078a9969d9a1a SHA-256 litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl 668169d35b87bf51324080390b1b1c5ab12bd335cfe5f1a99e3689abd5e02ae6 SHA-256 litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl 462d0c9f67ca522d9e0e4acd245e90b36ce0d5353604a66bb7c43a1ec4a6fcf7 SHA-256 litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl c2e32d0ce2548aa662c18bf5001911a79fe5b30cf8357132275add02fdcde054 SHA-256 litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-musllinux_1_2_aarch64.whl 1bbce8caa94f01c0aaa0b7ddae51553a8a32e1ce53d96d44fe583272aff7ad00 SHA-256 litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-musllinux_1_2_x86_64.whl 12d4ccc5c6f8d35cf4f2cf233b7f3e418e863e657d81ff5f5fc9e210005b9484 SHA-256 litellm-1.107.0-cp310-abi3-win_amd64.whl References LiteLLM, Contained: Oct 21, 2026 LiteLLM release v1.107.0 Compromised Python Software Foundation, Site-specific configuration hook . hypotheses.title: Initial access via the disclosed vulnerability affecting Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting the disclosed vulnerability in Microsoft 365 / Entra ID within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, supply-chain; impact: fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for the referenced CVE.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Microsoft 365 / Entra ID' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for the referenced CVE in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-the referenced CVE/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the the referenced CVE fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('the referenced CVE')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Microsoft 365 / Entra ID hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, supply-chain; impact: fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('cook.pth','cook.py','sitecustomize.py') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, supply-chain; impact: fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 Devices

article.raw_text: Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 Devices View CSAF Summary Nozomi Networks has published information on vulnerabilities in Nozomi Guardian/CMC. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products affected by these vulnerabilities. Siemens recommends to contact customer support to receive patch and update information. The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 Devices are affected: RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-33387, CVE-2026-33388, CVE-2026-33389, CVE-2026-33391, CVE-2026-33920) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.5 Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 4 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine, Incorrect Authorization, Lack of Administrator Control over Security, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-33387 A template injection vulnerability was discovered in the Dashboards functionality due to improper validation of an input parameter. An authenticated user with the required privileges can define a dashboard containing a malicious payload, or a victim can be socially engineered into importing a malicious dashboard. When the victim views or imports the dashboard, the payload executes in their browser context, allowing the attacker to modify application data or disrupt application availability. Read More 1 Affected Product RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-1336 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements Used in a Template Engine CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 4.6 MEDIUM CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33388 An access control vulnerability was discovered in the Credentials Manager functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. A remote authenticated user with limited privileges can view a limited subset of the available entries in the Credentials Manager. The actual credential values are not directly visible, but the user can delete entries or edit their properties. An attacker who deletes or edits an entry can disrupt authentication for dependent devices, and one who manipulates an entry's configuration may be able to indirectly obtain the credentials. Read More 2 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.4 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33389 An improper certificate/host key validation vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling functionality, which established encrypted connections to target devices without validating the remote host's identity, and no option was provided to enable it. A man-in-the-middle attacker positioned between a sensor and a polled device can, during a polling session, impersonate the device and intercept the communication, including the credentials used to access it. The captured credentials can then be replayed to authenticate against the device itself or against other devices sharing the same credentials, allowing the attacker to access and tamper with the device's data and to disrupt its operations. Read More 3 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-671 Lack of Administrator Control over Security CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.5 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33391 An access control vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling configuration functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. An authenticated user with limited privileges can remotely bypass the intended access control of the web management interface and modify the Smart Polling discovery configuration. This allows the attacker to disrupt the visibility of assets in the monitored network. Read More 4 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 5.4 MEDIUM CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L View CVE Details CVE-2026-33920 A cross-site request forgery vulnerability was discovered in the login functionality (both standard and SAML) due to missing validation of the anti-CSRF token. An attacker with a valid account can trick a victim into unknowingly authenticating with the attacker's credentials. Any operation performed by the victim in this state is attributed to the attacker's account, compromising the integrity of the audit trail. Read More 5 Affected Products RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Nozomi Guardian/CMC Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Contact customer support to receive patch and update information Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-352 Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 3.5 LOW CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments Siemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Advisory Conversion Disclaimer This ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-911336 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. This is republished to CISA's website as a means of increasing visibility and is provided "as-is" for informational purposes only. CISA is not responsible for the editorial or technical accuracy of republished advisories and provides no warranties of any kind regarding any information contained within this advisory. Further, CISA does not endorse any commercial product or service. Please contact Siemens ProductCERT directly for any questions regarding this advisory.
