hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-33387 affecting the affected product/service
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-33387 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-33387, CVE-2026-33388, CVE-2026-33389; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-33387.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-33387 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-33387/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-33387 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-33387')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-33387, CVE-2026-33388, CVE-2026-33389; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.siemens.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-33387, CVE-2026-33388, CVE-2026-33389; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Siemens SIMATIC S7 PLCs Web Server
article.summary: View CSAF Summary SIMATIC S7-1500 devices contain multiple vulnerabilities in the web server that could allow an attacker to execute malicious code in an authorized user’s browser session and perform PLC operations within the scope of that user’s authorization. Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. article.title: Tracking AI adoption in North Korean threat actor tradecraft
article.summary: As Microsoft Threat Intelligence continues to track how threat actors operationalize AI to increase the speed and efficiency of attacks, we’ve identified North Korean threat actors expanding their use of AI with varying levels of adoption. This blog breaks down how North Korean threat actors are utilizing AI across their operations, reflecting a broader trend of threat actors incorporating AI into their attack chains. The post Tracking AI adoption in North Korean threat actor tradecraft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .
article.raw_text: Tracking AI adoption in North Korean threat actor tradecraft As Microsoft Threat Intelligence continues to track how threat actors operationalize AI to increase the speed and efficiency of attacks, we’ve identified North Korean threat actors expanding their use of AI with varying levels of adoption. This blog breaks down how North Korean threat actors are utilizing AI across their operations, reflecting a broader trend of threat actors incorporating AI into their attack chains. The post Tracking AI adoption in North Korean threat actor tradecraft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog . In this article Stages of AI adoption by North Korean threat actors AI use across North Korean threat operations AI-assisted targeting and reconnaissance AI-assisted social engineering and identity deception AI-assisted software and tooling development AI-assisted operational scaling and analysis Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft Defender detections As Microsoft Threat Intelligence continues to track how threat actors operationalize AI to increase the speed, efficiency, and complexity of attacks, we’ve identified North Korean threat actors expanding their use of AI with varying levels of adoption. Threat actors use AI as a force multiplier across their operations, particularly to accelerate and scale established workflows. Recent activities illustrate this AI-enabled acceleration and scaling: Jade Sleet launched campaigns through three front companies in a single week, Onyx Sleet generated dozens of tailored lures in minutes, Coral Sleet rapidly built a new capability to trojanize private source code repositories, and Diamond Sleet used AI to enhance tailored targeting workflows, including persona development and front company creation. Further, Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet are leveraging the open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to conduct operations, further indicating North Korea’s willingness to quickly adopt new AI technologies for their operations. The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea operates under extensive international sanctions and uses cyber operations and other illicit mechanisms to evade these restrictions and advance state objectives. Within this operating environment, North Korean threat actors have demonstrated the willingness to adopt new technologies that help sustain or advance existing operations. AI adoption by North Korean threat actors therefore largely supports existing goals and targeting priorities rather than representing a shift in actor motivations. North Korean threat actors conduct cyber operations primarily to generate revenue for the regime, collect strategic intelligence, and, in some cases, pursue politically motivated disruptive or destructive objectives. Across these objectives, North Korean threat actor tradecraft remains grounded in social engineering, malware delivery, and the abuse of legitimate tools. These operations commonly target cryptocurrency and financial organizations, information technology companies and software supply chains, government entities, and education-related organizations. Despite threat actors’ adoption of AI, Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that AI-enabled operations remain human-directed and have not become fully autonomous. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses the overall adoption of AI across North Korean threat actors as high, with threat actors such as Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet demonstrating an established use of AI across all operational workflows, alongside increasing adoption across the broader North Korean threat actor set. This blog breaks down how North Korean threat actors are utilizing AI across their operations, reflecting a broader trend of threat actors incorporating AI into their attack chains. We also provide mitigation guidance and Microsoft Defender detections to help organizations defend against these threats. Stages of AI adoption by North Korean threat actors North Korean threat actors are increasingly integrating generative and agentic AI platforms into their operations, but the rate and maturity of adoption vary. Based on identified AI use, Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses high-impact North Korean threat actors across four stages of adoption: emerging, expanding, accelerating, and operationalized. Across these actors, AI use spans research, content generation, development, malware and tooling, infrastructure, and broader operational activities. Mapping high-impact North Korean threat actors by stages of AI adoption Operationalized: Threat actors at this stage have embedded AI into routine operational workflows, using it as an established part of their existing processes. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that the North Korean threat actors Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet have operationalized AI across their entire operations, which frequently encompass identity-based attacks built on deceptive social engineering. These attacks can be accelerated with AI capabilities that tailor lures or personas to the intended audience. Accelerating: Threat actors at this stage demonstrate rapid adoption of AI across multiple operational functions. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Diamond Sleet , Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet are at the accelerating stage of AI adoption. Expanding: Threat actors at this stage are expanding their use of AI across selected operational activities, but adoption is not yet embedded across broader workflows. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Emerald Sleet is at the expanding stage of AI adoption. While evidence suggests Emerald Sleet has incorporated AI into some workflows, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has not identified the same level of adoption and impact as other North Korean threat actors. Emerging: Threat actors at this stage demonstrate limited or experimental use of AI. At this time, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has not assessed any North Korean threat actors as operating at the emerging stage. AI use across North Korean threat operations Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified North Korean threat actors using AI platforms to support a range of operational activities, from reconnaissance to developing social engineering content, maintaining fraudulent identities, supporting tool development, and scaling repetitive operational tasks. Current evidence indicates that these actors primarily use AI to enhance existing tradecraft and operator productivity rather than to enable autonomous operations. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified North Korean threat actors leveraging the following AI-enabled tactics as part of their threat operations. AI-assisted targeting and reconnaissance Based on industry reporting and changes in targeting activity in 2026, North Korean threat actors are scaling reconnaissance capabilities by using generative AI platforms, including gathering information on target organizations prior to launching social engineering operations. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified that these actors: Research organizations and employees, then use information from this research to craft highly bespoke and convincing lures, target-specific infrastructure, and job applications Research wallets, exchanges, and decentralized finance (DeFi) and blockchain workflows, accelerating the development of domain knowledge needed to support targeted operations Explore vulnerabilities, APIs, security products, and cloud services, leading to a demonstrated change in the speed and sophistication of threat activity against specific technologies Research software development roles, job requirements, and technology organizations to support job searching, resume development, and persona alignment, resulting in rapid tailored persona or lure creation, application to newly posted job roles, or spear phishing operations For example, between June 8 and June 12, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified Jade Sleet conducting job-themed targeting against individuals across various organizations, including those involved in cybersecurity, AI, blockchain, and talent recruitment companies. The actor leveraged tailored domains, social media profiles, and industry-specific knowledge to pose as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company, using software engineer-themed opportunities to initiate contact and schedule interviews with individuals who engaged with the outreach. Within this short time frame, Jade Sleet conducted similar job-themed targeting using two additional front companies, supported by comparable infrastructure and relevant domain knowledge. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that the pace and breadth of this activity demonstrates how Jade Sleet is using generative AI to accelerate operational workflows, including rapidly developing target- and industry-specific knowledge, tailoring reconnaissance and targeting, and scaling outreach to target individuals. Jasper Sleet also continues to leverage generative AI platforms to build fake digital personas. The actor’s use of suspected generative and agentic AI-assisted resume workflows demonstrates an improvement in the speed, scale, and relevance of persona preparation over the past year. Identified application activity indicates that the actor has invested in repeatable tooling to support employment-themed operations, ultimately helping the actor scale application activity and interact more credibly with the hiring processes of impacted organizations. Since August 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed Diamond Sleet returning to targeting the oil and gas sector for the first time since 2023, expanding their focus on communications and internet policy-related organizations, and continuing to target defense-related organizations. Further, Diamond Sleet has created fake communications technology companies, complete with supporting websites and tailored personas, to target telecommunications companies under the guise of legitimate business partnerships. These shifts have occurred alongside Diamond Sleet’s increased use of generative AI platforms to support reconnaissance and technical development, suggesting that AI could be improving the efficiency of existing operational workflows. AI-assisted social engineering and identity deception Several North Korean threat actors leverage job-themed social engineering techniques to gain access to target environments. For example, Sapphire Sleet, Jade Sleet, and Coral Sleet use employment- and interview-themed social engineering to target users and organizations, while Jasper Sleet uses fraudulent identities to obtain legitimate remote employment. These actors leverage AI to improve the process of creating convincing lures, aid in the development of fake personas, and evade detection when interacting with targets. Specifically, these actors use AI to: Produce tailored phishing, recruiter, and investment lures Create job-themed payload-delivery content and malicious repository lures Translate content and adjust tone to support foreign-language impersonation and more natural communications Build resumes, biographies, and realistic interview responses Support coding assessments, job-related tasks, and the management of multiple worker personas Enhance profile images and other identity artifacts Alter profile images, video, voice, and backgrounds Sustain recruiter, developer, investor, and other social identities across interactions and platforms Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified over 100 PDF lure files attributed to Onyx Sleet that were created in August and September 2026 with target-specific details. Metadata indicated that the actor created dozens of files at a time in rapid succession within minutes, highly likely to be the output of an AI platform. This automation supports the actor’s high-volume phishing campaigns against South Korean users and could make disruption and detection efforts more difficult given the rapid regeneration or modification of additional lures. Microsoft Threat Intelligence has also identified possible synthetic media generation, focused on AI-created voice and video, by Emerald Sleet. While we have not been able to determine the full operational impact of such tooling, it is highly likely that synthetic media creation is valued by multiple North Korean threat actors, as it significantly enhances existing social engineering capabilities. AI-assisted software and tooling development Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified evidence indicating that North Korean threat actors are leveraging AI-enabled software and tools to assist in malware development. These tools include AI-assisted development platforms, such as Cursor, which have likely enabled Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet to: Generate, convert, debug, and refactor code Assist with scripts, commands, persistence mechanisms, and obfuscation Troubleshoot errors and help operators diagnose tool behavior Support the adaptation or reimplementation of functionality across languages, libraries, and environments Additionally, AI-enabled development cycles further allow threat actors to circumvent detection and blocking efforts, as AI platforms streamline retooling, helping enable threat actors to rapidly pivot in reaction to defensive measures. For example, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified evidence indicating that Sapphire Sleet, who has conducted several supply chain attacks, likely incorporated AI during the August 2026 Rust software compromise. The activity spanned from initial stages targeting Rust developers to development and deployment of malware. Notably, Sapphire Sleet’s malware in this campaign was a marked improvement compared with other attributed campaigns, as the malware used dynamic .NET compilation during post-exploitation, most likely for defense evasion. And, since April 2026, Coral Sleet has operationalized a workflow to trojanize private GitHub repositories, integrating them into their existing malware chain. This new capability, its breadth and scale, and its rapid implementation were highly likely engineered using an AI-enabled development platform. AI-assisted operational scaling and analysis North Korean threat actors are leveraging AI platforms to scale and manage diverse operations. For example, Jasper Sleet’s AI tooling helps maintain consistent communication and performance across multiple fraudulent worker personas. We have also seen evidence of AI use for automating repetitive tasks, summarizing collected information from victim organizations, and accelerating post-compromise decision making while human operators likely continue to direct intent and objectives. This operational adoption extends to emerging agentic AI technologies. Since late October 2026, Microsoft threat Intelligence has identified Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet leveraging open-source agentic AI penetration testing ARTEX in operations, highlighting how North Korean threat actors are adopting new AI technologies as they become available. Mitigation and protection guidance Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI . The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender , Microsoft Entra , and Microsoft Purview . This allows organizations to understand what AI assets exist in their environment, recognize emerging risk patterns, and prioritize governance and security across AI agents, applications, and platforms. To learn more about the Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI see: Assess your organization’s AI risk with Microsoft Security Dashboard for AI . Additionally, Microsoft Agent 365 serves as a control plane for AI agents in enterprise environments, allowing users to manage, govern, and secure AI agents and workflows while monitoring emerging risks of agentic AI use. Agent 365 supports a growing ecosystem of agents, including Microsoft agents, broader ecosystems of agents such as Adobe and Databricks, and open-source agents published on GitHub. As the AI-enabled operations conducted by North Korean threat actors vary across TTPs, the following guidance can help organizations harden their networks against multiple classes of threats. Vulnerability and exposure management Use Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management to identify, assess, remediate, and track vulnerabilities across critical assets. Use the exposure score to reduce your vulnerability exposure and the Microsoft Secure Score to identify and remediate security misconfigurations in your environment. Use a perimeter scanning tool like Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management to understand your organization’s digital footprint and potential attack surface. Targeting web-facing vulnerabilities continues to be one of the most effective attack methods for initial access. Ensure any web-facing systems are isolated from the public internet with a secure network boundary and access them with a virtual private network (VPN). If certain servers must be accessible on the public internet, position them behind a web application firewall (WAF) , reverse proxy , or perimeter network (also known as a DMZ), which can reduce the risk of vulnerability exploitation in some cases. Consider automating patching where possible. Windows Update client policies offer automated patching, which can greatly reduce the amount of time IT admins must spend identifying, configuring, and deploying updates. To help manage infrastructure distributed across cloud, on-premises, and hybrid networks, use a centralized patching solution like Azure Update Manager . Protecting against social engineering and phishing Educate users about protecting personal and business information on social media, filtering unsolicited communication, identifying lures in spear-phishing emails and watering holes, and reporting reconnaissance attempts and other suspicious activity. Educate users about preventing malware infections , such as ignoring or deleting unsolicited and unexpected emails or attachments sent through instant messaging applications or social networks. Review the recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 to ensure your organization has established essential defenses and knows how to monitor and respond to threat activity. Invest in user awareness training and phishing simulations. Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender for Office 365, which also includes simulating phishing messages in Microsoft Teams, is one approach to running realistic attack scenarios in your organization. Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) in Defender for Office 365 to quarantine sent mail in response to newly acquired threat intelligence and retroactively neutralize malicious phishing, spam, or malware messages that have already been delivered to mailboxes. Responders could also manually check for and purge unwanted emails containing URLs and/or Subject fields that are similar, but not identical, to those of known bad messages. Investigate malicious email that was delivered in Microsoft 365 and use Threat Explorer to find and delete phishing emails. Turn on Safe Links and Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Only allow device code flow where necessary. Microsoft recommends blocking device code flow wherever possible . Where necessary, configure Microsoft Entra ID’s device code flow in your Conditional Access policies. Vetting potential employees Exercise greater scrutiny for employees of staffing companies, since this is the easiest avenue for North Korean workers to infiltrate target companies. Check to make sure a potential employee’s social media/professional accounts are not highly similar to the accounts of other individuals. In addition, check that a contact phone number listed on a potential employee’s account is unique and not also used by other accounts. Scrutinize resumes and background checks for consistency of names, addresses, and dates. Consider contacting references by phone or video-teleconference rather than email only. Search whether a potential employee is employed at multiple companies using the same persona. Ensure the potential employee is seen on camera during multiple video telecommunication sessions. If the potential employee reports video and/or microphone issues that prohibit participation, this should be considered a red flag. Confirm the potential employee has a digital footprint. This includes a real phone number (not VOIP), a residential address, and social media accounts. Defending against malware Turn on cloud-delivered protection in Microsoft Defender Antivirus or the equivalent for your antivirus product to cover rapidly evolving attacker tools and techniques. Cloud-based machine learning protections block a majority of new and unknown variants. Ensure Microsoft Defender Antivirus definitions are up to date and real-time protection is turned on . Run endpoint detection and response (EDR) in block mode so that Microsoft Defender for Endpoint can block malicious artifacts, even when your non-Microsoft antivirus does not detect the threat or when Microsoft Defender Antivirus is running in passive mode. EDR in block mode works behind the scenes to remediate malicious artifacts that are detected post-breach. Configure investigation and remediation in full automated mode to let Microsoft Defender for Endpoint take immediate action on alerts to resolve breaches, significantly reducing alert volume. Configure automatic attack disruption in Microsoft Defender XDR. Automatic attack disruption is designed to contain attacks in progress, limit the impact on an organization’s assets, and provide more time for security teams to remediate the attack fully. Enable network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. Microsoft Defender XDR customers can turn on attack surface reduction rules to prevent several of the infection vectors of this threat. These rules, which can be configured by users with administrator rights, offer significant hardening against targeted attacks. In observed attacks, Microsoft customers who had the following rules turned on could mitigate the attack in the initial stages and prevent hands-on-keyboard activity: Block executable content from email client and webmail Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts Use advanced protection against ransomware Microsoft Defender detections Microsoft Defender customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. Tactic Observed activity Microsoft Defender coverage Actor-specific alerts Known threat actor activity Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Emerald Sleet threat actor activity – Diamond Sleet Actor activity detected – Onyx Sleet activity group – Pearl Sleet actor activity detected – Sapphire Sleet actor activity – Jade Sleet threat actor activity detected – Coral Sleet activity Reconnaissance AI-assisted research of target organizations Microsoft Defender for Cloud – Possible AI Tools Reconnaissance Detected – Possible Secret Reconnaissance Detected Initial access Sign-in activity; phishing Microsoft Defender XDR – Sign-in activity by a suspected North Korean entity Jasper Sleet Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Atypical travelImpossible travel – Microsoft Entra threat intelligence (sign-in) Microsoft Defender for Office 365 – A potentially malicious URL click was detected – A user clicked through to a potentially malicious URL – Suspicious email sending patterns detected – Email messages containing malicious URL removed after delivery – Email messages removed after delivery – Email reported by user as malware or phish Execution Backdoors observed in Sapphire Sleet Rust software compromise Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Trojan:Linux/ProcmacSteal – Trojan:PowerShell/ProcmacSteal – Trojan:MacOS/ProcmacSteal – Trojan:Cargo/ProcmacSteal Microsoft Security Copilot Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports. Customers can also deploy AI agents , including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents , to perform security tasks efficiently: Threat Intelligence Briefing agent Phishing Triage agent Threat Hunting agent Dynamic Threat Detection agent Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs. Threat intelligence reports Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use the following threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments. Threat overview profile: Threat actors operationalizing AI Actor profile: Coral Sleet Actor profile: Diamond Sleet Actor profile: Emerald Sleet Actor profile: Jade Sleet Actor profile: Jasper Sleet Actor profile: Onyx Sleet Actor profile: Pearl Sleet Actor profile: Sapphire Sleet Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the Microsoft Security Copilot integration in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the embedded experience in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about this threat. Learn more For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog . To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn , X (formerly Twitter) , and Bluesky . hypotheses.title: Initial access via the disclosed vulnerability affecting Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting the disclosed vulnerability in Microsoft 365 / Entra ID within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, supply-chain; impact: ransomware, fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Microsoft 365 / Entra ID
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Microsoft 365 / Entra ID, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for the referenced CVE.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Microsoft 365 / Entra ID' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for the referenced CVE in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-the referenced CVE/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the the referenced CVE fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('the referenced CVE')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Microsoft 365 / Entra ID hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Post-foothold lateral movement consistent with the reported actor
hypotheses.statement: An attacker who matched the TTPs of the reported actor has moved laterally inside the estate using RDP/SMB/WinRM, admin tooling, or Kerberos abuse.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'lateral_movement' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, supply-chain; impact: ransomware, fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: Anomalous remote logons (Type 3 / Type 10)
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4624 logon-type 3/10 events show no bursts from a single source to many destinations, lateral movement via RDP/SMB is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id in (4624) and logon_type in (3,10) | summarize dests = dcount(dst_host) by src_user, src_host | where dests > 10

objectives.title: Admin-tool usage outside baseline
objectives.falsification_criterion: If PsExec / WMIC / PowerShell remoting / Impacket-style usage is absent outside known admin jump-hosts, the lateral-tool hypothesis is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('psexec.exe','psexesvc.exe','wmic.exe','wsmprovhost.exe') and host !in (admin_jumphosts)

objectives.title: Kerberos abuse telemetry
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4769 ticket requests show no anomalous RC4 / odd-SPN patterns and no AS-REP roasting indicators, credential-based lateral movement is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id == 4769 and ticket_encryption == 'RC4-HMAC' | summarize by target_spn, account_name

objectives.title: Lateral file-copy staging
objectives.falsification_criterion: If SMB writes of archives / executables across multiple hosts from one user/host are absent, lateral staging is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: file | where action == 'write' and ext in ('.7z','.rar','.zip','.exe') and dest matches /\\\\.*\\(C\$|admin\$)/

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on vectors: phishing, exploit, supply-chain; impact: ransomware, fraud; products: Microsoft 365 / Entra ID.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is aware of OS command injection and Dirty Frag vulnerabilities that affect CoreTec product versions listed in this document. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could result in impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability of the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation. The following versions of Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product are affected: CoreTec5 vers:CoreTec5/ CoreTec4 vers:CoreTec4/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Hitachi Energy CoreTec5 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection'), Write-what-where Condition Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Switzerland Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-13162 An OS command vulnerability exists in CoreTec product that allows authenticated users with certain roles to execute arbitrary system commands with full control over the device. The vulnerability exists in the configuration daemon's time synchronization handler, which is responsible for setting the system timezone. When processing timezone configuration updates, the daemon constructs a shell command by concatenating user-supplied input without any sanitization or validation. Read More 2 Affected Products CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations Vendor fix Updat
article.raw_text: Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is aware of OS command injection and Dirty Frag vulnerabilities that affect CoreTec product versions listed in this document. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could result in impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability of the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation. The following versions of Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product are affected: CoreTec5 vers:CoreTec5/ CoreTec4 vers:CoreTec4/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Hitachi Energy CoreTec5 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection'), Write-what-where Condition Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Switzerland Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-13162 An OS command vulnerability exists in CoreTec product that allows authenticated users with certain roles to execute arbitrary system commands with full control over the device. The vulnerability exists in the configuration daemon's time synchronization handler, which is responsible for setting the system timezone. When processing timezone configuration updates, the daemon constructs a shell command by concatenating user-supplied input without any sanitization or validation. Read More 2 Affected Products CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations Vendor fix Update to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0 CoreTec4 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations Vendor fix Upgrade to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0 Mitigation Follow general mitigation factors Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-78 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection') CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.5 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 4.0 7.7 HIGH CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N View CVE Details CVE-2026-43284 A vulnerability exists in the IPsec ESP subsystem (esp4) of the Linux kernel used in CoreTec5 that allows a local unprivileged user to escalate privileges to root. The flaw exists in how the kernel handles memory pages when processing ESP encrypted network packets. An attacker can craft a packet that causes the kernel to decrypt data directly into memory pages it does not own, including cached copies of privileged operating system binaries. When one of those binaries is executed, the attacker's injected code runs with root privileges. In CoreTec5, the vulnerable ESP component is compiled in kernel as a built-in and is present at boot time allowing a local user to exploit it. Read More 3 Affected Products CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations Vendor fix Update to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0 CoreTec4 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations Vendor fix Update to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0 Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-123 Write-what-where Condition CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 8.8 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H View CVE Details Acknowledgments Ritesh Kumar Kalle, Subhojeet Mukherjee, Hishamudeen of the Cybersecurity Research group, Hitachi India R&D Center reported these vulnerabilities to CISA. This document and parts hereof must not be reproduced or copied without written permission from Hitachi Energy and the contents hereof must not be imparted to a third party nor used for any unauthorized purpose. All rights to registrations and trademarks reside with their respective owners. Support For additional information and support please contact your product provider or Hitachi Energy service organization. For contact information, see https://www.hitachienergy.com/contact-us/ for Hitachi Energy contact-centers. General Mitigation Factors Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect a process control network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Process control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Proper password policies and processes should be followed. Additional information on Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices can be found in the Hitachi Energy “Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices” Cybersecurity Notification. [1] SSVC SSVCv2/E:N/A:N/2026-10-26T15:17:24Z/ Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-13162 affecting Linux kernel
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-13162 in Linux kernel within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-13162, CVE-2026-43284; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; products: Linux kernel.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Linux kernel
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Linux kernel, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-13162.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Linux kernel' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-13162 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-13162/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-13162 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-13162')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Linux kernel hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-13162, CVE-2026-43284; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; products: Linux kernel.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.hitachienergy.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-13162, CVE-2026-43284; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; products: Linux kernel.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-111357 Ivanti Connect Secure Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability CVE-2026-97229 GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . article.title: The Classics Return: Vulnerable E-Mail Scripts, (Wed, Nov 4th)
article.summary: One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. The vulnerability was pretty straightforward: Adding additional parameters to the URL leaked environment variables. Other vulnerabilities allowed setting the "To" address and were heavily abused by spammers. And if parameters were passed directly to the sendmail binary, similar vulnerabilities could allow arbitrary code execution.
article.raw_text: The Classics Return: Vulnerable E-Mail Scripts, (Wed, Nov 4th) One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. The vulnerability was pretty straightforward: Adding additional parameters to the URL leaked environment variables. Other vulnerabilities allowed setting the "To" address and were heavily abused by spammers. And if parameters were passed directly to the sendmail binary, similar vulnerabilities could allow arbitrary code execution. One of the early web application vulnerabilities I remember was CVE-2000-0411 [CVE]. This was a simple vulnerability in a CGI-bin script used to send e-mail. The vulnerability was pretty straightforward: Adding additional parameters to the URL leaked environment variables. Other vulnerabilities allowed setting the "To" address and were heavily abused by spammers. And if parameters were passed directly to the sendmail binary, similar vulnerabilities could allow arbitrary code execution. Today, I noticed a slight resurgence in scans targeting e-mail scripts on our honeypots. Today, there are numerous scripts like the old "formail" scripts, and it is hard to link a specific vulnerability to any of these scans. But my main suspect is spammers looking for webforms that allow setting arbitrary "To" headers. The URLs I am seeing: "/sendmail.php" "/test-mail.php" "/testemail.php" "/config/mail_config.php" "/mail_config.php" "/email-test.php" "/mailtest.php" In particular, the "Test" part of the filename suggests that the attacker is not looking for production scripts, but for test scripts left behind during development. This, along with the requests for credential/secret files that top our "Leaderboard," points to a more fundamental issue: Code hygiene. Do not leave behind development artifacts that should never have reached a live website. For example, some excerpts from a random "mailtest.php" script that came back in a Google search [mailtest]: /* DONT FORGET TO DELETE THIS SCRIPT WHEN FINISHED! */ $server = array( 'HTTP_HOST', 'SERVER_NAME', 'SERVER_ADDR', 'SERVER_PORT', 'SERVER_ADMIN', 'SERVER_SIGNATURE', 'SERVER_SOFTWARE', 'REMOTE_ADDR', 'DOCUMENT_ROOT', 'REQUEST_URI', 'SCRIPT_NAME', 'SCRIPT_FILENAME', ); $to = ( isset( $_GET['email'] ) ? $_GET['email'] : FALSE ); $subject = 'Mail Test Successful for ' . $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']; $message = ''; ??????? foreach ( $server as $s ) { $message .= sprintf( '%s: %s', $s, $_SERVER[$s] ) . PHP_EOL; }; $success = mail( $to, $subject, $message, $headers ); The comment at the top says it all: This is not meant for production use, and even on a development site, it should likely be deployed only briefly for debugging. The script takes any "To" address from the "email" GET parameter and exfiltrates/displays part of the server configuration. It can be useful to scan your own hosts for some of these URLs as an additional control, but you really want to catch these issues during application deployment. [CVE] https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2000-0411 [mailtest] https://gist.github.com/Porrapat/60ed7411d933122fc481 -- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter | (c) SANS Internet Storm Center. https://isc.sans.edu Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 United States License.

article.title: Mutipath TCP: Use and Detection, (Mon, Nov 2nd)
article.summary: Last week, an often-ignored&#;x26;#;xc2;&#;x26;#;xa0;TCP option, introduced in 2020, made the news due to a new vulnerability in Linux&#;x26;#;39;s implementation (RFC&#;x26;#;xc2;&#;x26;#;xa0;8684, &#;x26;#;xc2;&#;x26;#;xa0;CVE-2026-98432)
article.raw_text: Mutipath TCP: Use and Detection, (Mon, Nov 2nd) Last week, an often-ignored&#;x26;#;xc2;&#;x26;#;xa0;TCP option, introduced in 2020, made the news due to a new vulnerability in Linux&#;x26;#;39;s implementation (RFC&#;x26;#;xc2;&#;x26;#;xa0;8684, &#;x26;#;xc2;&#;x26;#;xa0;CVE-2026-98432) Last week, an often-ignored TCP option, introduced in 2020, made the news due to a new vulnerability in Linux's implementation (RFC 8684, CVE-2026-98432) Instead of looking at the vulnerability, I am using this diary to talk a bit about multipath TCP (MPTCP) and how you may see it used in your network. What is MPTCP? Traditionally, TCP is a connection-oriented protocol. Connections are established between a client and server, and host IP addresses are not expected to change for a specific connection. This restriction to a specific path does not always match modern system architecture. For example, mobile devices may switch from a local WIFI network to a cellular network at any time. Having to re-establish TCP connections may break applications. At the same time, servers often have a hard time "filling" high-bandwidth links using a single TCP connection due to limits on Window Size and the sequence number range [RFC 6182]. MPTCP is supposed to solve these problems by allowing connections to be split and handed over between different IP addresses. The only widely used implementation I have observed is iOS/iPadOS. In this case, IPv4 connections to Apple (17.0.0.0/8) often utilize MPTCP [Apple]. MPTCP was initially used for Siri, and later for other services like Apple Music. Two versions of MPTCP are currently defined and used: v0 and v1. At first, MPTCP Options The MPTCP Option (0x1e, 30) is followed by a byte containing 4 bits indicating the subtype and 4 bits indicating the version (0 or 1). +----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+ | TCP Option | Option Length|Subtype| Version| Flags | +----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+ | 30 | variable | | 0 or 1 | | +----------------+--------------+----------------+----------------+ MP_CAPABLE (subtype 0) : Indicates MPTCP support. Both sides must include it in the TCP handshake for MPTCP support to be enabled. Each MP_CAPABLE option also carries an 8-byte key that will later be used to identify and authenticate the different sub-sessions. MP_JOIN (subtype 1): A second TCP connection may join an initial connection using the MP_JOIN option. This connection will typically be initiated by the client, but may originate from a different IP address. The RFC does specifically allow the server to initiate the second (or additional) connection. The RFC states: "It is permissible for either host in a connection to initiate the creation of a new subflow, but it is expected that this will normally be the original connection initiator." Ports should be the same, but do not have to be. Of course, this also accounts for common firewall rules. The web server will likely listen only on port 443, and the client's firewall will reject inbound SYN packets. DSS (Data Sequence Signal, subtype 2): Each TCP connection which is part of MPTCP maintains its own sequence numbers, and acts just like any other "normal" TCP connection. To stitch the content of multiple connections together, the DSS option is used. It maps the respective's TCP sequence numbers to the sequence numbers of the combined connection. ADD_ADDR/REMOVE_ADDR (subtypes 3, 4): these options are somewhat similar to MP_JOIN, but instead of actually setting up an additional connection, they advertise (or remove) additional addresses or ports that can be used. MPTCP Detection The best way to detect MPTCP is to look for TCP Option 30. Here are a few ways to do so: Wireshark/tshark: Wireshark has a "mptcp" display filter keyword. As so often, Wireshark does make it easy. tcpdump: There is no great way to match TCP options in tcpdump. But MPTCP packets, particularly SYN packets, tend to have large TCP headers, so a quick match on TCP header length can help. For example: 'tcp[12]>0xd0' Suricata: Use the "tcp.hdr" keyword to inspect TCP options. The tricky part is that the option length isn't always the same. But there should be at least one MP_CAPABLE message that includes both the sender and receiver key, making this option 20 bytes long. The first three bytes are |1e 14 00| for version 0 or |1e 14 01| for version 1. Snort: Snort does not have a keyword to inspect TCP options, and as far as I know, no way to filter for multipath TCP. The snort_decoder "experimental TCP option" alert only triggers on specific option types reserved for experimental use. Zeek: By default, zeek does not log options, but it does offer the tcp_option and tcp_options events that can easily be used to log MPTCP. For example: event tcp_option(c: connection, is_orig: bool, opt: count, optlen: count) { if ( opt == 30 ) { print(fmt("MPTCP between %s and %s", c$id$orig_h, c$id$resp_h)); } } [Apple] https://support.apple.com/en-us/101905 [RFC8694] https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8684 [CVE-2026-98432] https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/10/30/1 -- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter | (c) SANS Internet Storm Center. https://isc.sans.edu Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 United States License.

article.summary: Building your malware analysis lab is a key point before playing with malware. Today, thanks to virtualization, it&#;x26;#;39;s convenient to play with snapshots in your lab. Start a new investigation from a clean snapshot and take some more when you reached a critical step. But, if you need to revert to a previous snapshot, all changes applied to the VM are... lost! But, if you need to revert to a previous snapshot, all changes applied to the VM are... lost! Therefore, it&#;x26;#;39;s important to store important data outside the VM. Building your malware analysis lab is a key point before playing with malware. Today, thanks to virtualization, it's convenient to play with snapshots in your lab. Start a new investigation from a clean snapshot and take some more when you reached a critical step. But, if you need to revert to a previous snapshot, all changes applied to the VM are... lost! Therefore, it's important to store important data outside the VM. If you do malware analysis with Ghidra[ 1 ], your work lives in "projects". A project is a ".gpr" file and a ".rep" directory sitting on the disk of your analysis machine. Every renamed function, comment, structure and bookmark you added is stored there. And,as said before, hours of work can be lost if your VM has issues or you restart to a clean snapshot. When you create a new project in Ghidra, it always asks you if you want a "shared" or "non-shared" project: Ghidra ships with a component that many people ignore: Ghidra Server. It is included in the standard distribution (no extra download, no licence) and turns your local projects into "shared projects" backed by a central repository. Here are some reasons why it's useful to deploy one in yout lab: Persistence : revert your VMs as often as you want; the annotated programs are safe on the server. Versioning : each check-in creates a new version of the program with a comment. You can go back to a previous state of your analysis or compare versions (like a git repot) Multiple clients : start an analysis on one box and continue it on another one (another VM, your laptop, a colleague's workstation). Collaboration : several analysts can work on the same samples, with read-only, read/write or admin permissions per repository. Confidentiality : everything stays in your lab. No sample or customer-related binary is pushed to a third-party service. This matters when you handle files coming from incident response engagements. From a requirements perspective, the server is lightweight. I'm running Ghidra 12.1.4 in an Ubuntu container on my Proxmox host, but any small Linux VM will do. Recommended specs: Small Linux VM or container, kept separate from your analysis VMs 2 x CPU, 4GB (enough for small teams, personal use) 8G of storage (may depends on your volume of samples!) JDK 21 or newer To avoid incompatibility issues, use the same version of Ghida between the server and clients. Keep versions aligned! Important remarks about networking: Ports TCP/13100 & TCP/13101 must be reachable from clients Clients must be able to resolve the hostname announced by the server Don't forget that this server will host malicious pieces of code! Treat it as hosting live malware and keep it in your malware analysis lab network! Nothing is executed there, but the repositories contain the raw bytes of every sample you imported. Sounds legit but never expose it to the Internet. Ghidra Server is a Java RMI service. The basic setup is pretty easy. There is no official container image, but the distribution contains everything needed to run the server as a regular service. First, create a dedicated account, unpack Ghidra and create the repositories directory: # apt install openjdk-25-jre-headless unzip # useradd -r -m -d /opt/ghidra -s /usr/sbin/nologin ghidra # cd /opt && unzip ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC_*.zip # ln -s ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC ghidra-current # mkdir -p /opt/ghidra-repos && chown -R ghidra: /opt/ghidra-repos The configuration is in "server/server.conf". Set the repositories directory, the account used to run the JVM, and the server parameters: ghidra.repositories.dir=/opt/ghidra-repos ???????wrapper.app.account=ghidra # Authentication: local Ghidra passwords, expire after 90 days wrapper.app.parameter.1=-a0 wrapper.app.parameter.2=-e90 # Hostname announced to clients wrapper.app.parameter.3=-ip wrapper.app.parameter.4=ghidra.lab.local # Repositories directory (must be the last parameter) wrapper.app.parameter.5=${ghidra.repositories.dir} The main authentication modes are "-a0" (passwords managed by the server), "-a2" (PKI with client certificates) and "-a4" (JAAS, to plug into LDAP or Active Directory). Leave anonymous access disabled. I'm using the local authentication scheme (-a0). The "-ip" parameter is important: RMI returns this name to the clients, which reconnect to it on ports 13101 and 13102. If clients can't resolve it, they reach the server on the first port and then fail. If you want to bind the service to a single interface (your VPN interface, for example), add -i . Install the service, check it and create the users: # /opt/ghidra-current/server/svrInstall # systemctl status ghidraSvr # ss -tlnp | grep -E '1310[0-2]' # cd /opt/ghidra-current/server # ./svrAdmin -add xavier # ./svrAdmin -list -users New users get the initial password "changeme" (yes, unsecure...) and must change it at first login. The svrAdmin commands are queued and processed by the running server within a few seconds. Now, you are ready to use your brand now server! Repositories are created from the Ghidra client: File > New Project... and select "Shared Project". Enter the server name (the one used with -ip ) and port 13100, then log in. Click "Create Repository" and give it a name (mine is " MalwareLab" ). The user who creates it becomes its administrator. Choose a local directory and a project name. This is your local working copy. Access for other analysts is managed from the client (Project > Edit Access List) or from the server, once the repository exists: # ./svrAdmin -grant john +w MalwareLab # +r read-only, +w read/write, +a admin A shared project still creates a . gpr file and a .rep d irectory locally! That's expected: they contain the connection settings, a cache and your checked-out copies. Importing a binary does not send it to the server. It remains a private file until you right-click it and select "Add to Version Control...". From then on, the workflow is similar to any source control system: Check Out a program to work on it (exclusively or not). Check In your changes with a comment; each check-in creates a new version. Versioned files display a version icon in the project tree; files without it are still local only. Project > Project Info shows the server and repository you are connected to. How to restore your project if your analysis VM has been reverted to a clean snapshot and the local project is gone? To get everything back, create a new Shared Project, connect to the server and select your existing repository (don't create a new one). The project tree is populated with all checked-in programs. If a file is still checked out by the old instance of the VM, right-click it, select View Checkouts and terminate the stale entry. What the server can't give back: Private files never added to version control. Changes made after the last check-in. Your client settings (tool layouts, key bindings, script directories, extensions), stored in ~/.config/ghidra/ . Your client certificate and key if you use PKI authentication. Back them up separately! Before deploying your own server, you can have a look at the ghidra-server project[ 2 ] that offers a free server for the RE community. But don't forget that, like any "cloud" service, you'll share your data! Happy reversing!
