hypotheses.title: Initial access via the disclosed vulnerability affecting Active Directory
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting the disclosed vulnerability in Active Directory within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; impact: fraud; products: Active Directory.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Active Directory
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of Active Directory, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for the referenced CVE.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Active Directory' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for the referenced CVE in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-the referenced CVE/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the the referenced CVE fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('the referenced CVE')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Active Directory hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; impact: fraud; products: Active Directory.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('server.conf','ghidra.repositories.dir','wrapper.app.account') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; impact: fraud; products: Active Directory.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-41709 Broadcom VMWare ESX Insufficient Logging Vulnerability CVE-2026-46300 Linux Kernel Missing Initialization of a Variable Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . article.title: Looking for a Language [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 21st)
article.summary: [This is a Guest Diary by Jeffray Spence, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]
article.raw_text: Looking for a Language [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 21st) [This is a Guest Diary by Jeffray Spence, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] [This is a Guest Diary by Jeffray Spence, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] Around Here, we start our day with coffee, but our day does not begin until we have our data...So much data. Where to even begin? When approaching a massive dataset, such as those from a DShield SIEM Honeypot, the first step is to actually find something to analyze. As for myself, I usually go looking for something that makes me go; " Huh. " Today we will be walking through a starting approach with Kibana Discover to search out embedded language preferences in webtraffic, then we will use this as a starting point for finding anomalous activity. Find A Problem to Get Some Data Inside of my DShield SIEM there are nearly a million records, so I approach by looking for a slightly smaller data carve with which to work which still represents the problem set: Anyone with Elastic Kibana can perform this approach on their webtraffic data as long as the HTTP headers are provided. Here, the logs are from my SANS Dshield Honeypot and the accompanying Dshield SIEM. For those who desire to install this setup there are plenty of great resources out there with links at the end of this article [ 1 ] [ 2 ]. In slightly more than 3 weeks of observation the rasperry pi honeypot had transferred a Million Records into the Elastic SIEM. These many records can prove very challenging when figuring out where to start, so it is helpful to know that even with no filtering applied on the Discover page the Field Statistics will give some fairly detailed metrics about what fields exist in the current Index. On the Discover page in the upper right, I selected my index (here the index is “ cowrie ”) and without any filter applied I selected Field Statistics : Calculating statistics ourselves is possible using ESQL and Stats, however this feature of Elastic makes gaining visibility much more obtainable at the onset. We are immediately presented with a screen displaying all of the Documents broken down by Top Values which potentially gives us some valuable insight: The resultant statistics show that in these 3 weeks my honeypot had generated 960,000 logs, but all of those are only within 4 rules. Four is less than a 960,000 so this gives a more manageable starting dataset: “ Huh. ” This little raspberry PI has been humming away quietly all day and all night and only 4 rules have popped up. I found this interesting. With no filtering applied only 15,271 records triggered any rule? This setup is a honeypot, so literally every record is suspicious. So, what about the other 944,866 records which triggered no rules? Today, we want a problem not a project, so we are going to use one of these rules to narrow down our traffic for analysis. We have rule triggers for the Index page . Boring. Great for generating a large dataset, but this is not a very targeted approach. Git Config is something I had previously analyzed, and this led me to discover malicious traffic attempting to scrape Git Config from internet hosts. Neat, but not for today. Fortinet Emulation , for those who don't know, has fairly recently gotten a lot of attention [ 3 ]. Only one detection so far in my honeypot, so for me that's just an outlier. Interesting, but not much of a corpus. Through the process of elimination, we are left with the Sonicwall Appliance Login Page rule. Good representation over the problem space with 41 individual hosts logging in activity. This could potentially demonstrate how an attack is conducted or give a clue as to who was conducting one. Perfect because we are looking for regular and repeating attack attempts. I selected these criteria as a Kibana filter. Now to start digging. Data Selection Now that we have a smaller dataset to work within, we need to decide what we want to find. After that we need to figure out how to actually find that. This first approach is what I would NOT recommend One do: Noticing here that every field statistic for all 157 records has One Distinct Value and only1 category under Distribution tells us these fields are ALL common to ALL records. A field common to every record will have a unique value for each record. We don't want common, we want weird: the approach I will use is to flip it and look at Distribution 2 or higher. This is Long tail analysis: Here we see the Distinct values are now descending with the “sweet spot” between 2 and 6 so. Not an exact criterion, but one that is practical for manual review. Within these fields we have fields of interest: When fields contain similar values, they may illustrate a relationship between the data represented. Here the traffic triggering the Sonicwall Rule contains a relatively small subset of unique values. The next step is to find something we cannot readily explain away; a simple exercise to conduct on the “ tags ”, “ host.ip ”, and “ host.mac ” fields. The IP and MAC are going to be both interfaces of my Dshield Pi itself, while the Tags are going to be metadata about how the rules generate. The “ source.geo.continent_code ” is not very useful in a Virtual Private Server (VPS) enabled world but may prove useful later. This leaves 2 fields: http.request.connection " Close " and " close ". Most traffic parsing tools are going to convert these all to lowercase string, and thus never see this small difference. . No longer interesting. http.request.mime_type " utf-8 " (the defacto choice) verses some interesting mime encoding... Next was to break down what this mime encoding is saying: " GBK,utf-8;q=0.7,*;q=0.3 " This string is sent to a webserver as the Accept-Charset HTTP header. Values of GBK,utf-8 , and wildcard ( * ) are present. The preference weights are specified as " q " (for “quality value” by convention). Since the implicit maximum weight value is q=1.0, the simplified character set preferences are: ( GBK;q=1.0),(utf-8;q=0.7),(*;q=0.3 ) I think of this as a preference for what character encoding to use: ( Send me “GBK” 100% of the time, if not “utf-8” 70%, and if not Whatever 30% ) UTF-8 makes sense as does wildcard ( * ). However, GBK is explicitly the extension of the “GB 2312” character set for Simplified Chinese characters. "Huh. " Why do these requests explicitly state they greatly desire to transfer data to my Honeypot, which is not in China, using an exclusively Chinese character set? I also apply this as a filter in Kibana to narrow our results to 8 Records: Two issues are now present. This dataset of 8 records is too narrow to work with, and also, we don’t actually care about the Sonicwall rule anymore now that we find some interesting traffic. Next, we need to pull in some additional data for this mime type field. Finding commonality So my Elastic SIEM, the webhoneypot index is for Webserver Logs, and my cowrie index shares these fields. Here the filter works for both. At this point we are not interested in the “Sonicwall Appliance” filter anymore, so we remove it. We are now using the “Mime Type” field to work out the language preferences and have 47 interesting records within the http.request.mime_type : These records now represent every inbound connection attempt sending this exact same format string for the GBK Character set preferences. There are 47 requests in total which send the identical preference header. How can we use this header to find odd traffic in our data? The problem set has not changed, only our dataset. We repeat the same process of sorting the Distribution Field under the Field statistics section. Following this Distribution Analysis process we see two User-Agents, which is interesting. However, we also very clearly see there are two source.geo.region_name values: “ Beijing ”, yeah, ok that makes sense. Beijing is in China… but “ Ontario ”? " Huh ". People do move around, however, following a purely statistical analysis approach one would not anticipate that Canadian Cyber actors would greatly desire a Chinese Character set while targeting my American Honeypot. This presents as an anomaly. We add the source.geo.region_name : Ontario filter and observe there are now only 3 records: At this point I exported these three records to Libre Office so I could look at them: Modern VPS availability makes the Autonomous System (AS) number far more useful than an IP: AS-7456 is the system responsible for all three of these records. This field, “source.geo.as.number” will be our next field to analyze: What’s Your Number? We now set our new filter to be source.geo.as.number : 7456 We remove all other filters and follow the same “Distribution Analysis” as before. We immediately find the same pattern: There is again a language preference but this time in a different field: The http.request.accept-language encoding for all 31 requests from AS-7456 read as either: zh-CN,zh;q=0.9,en;q=0.8,en-GB;q=0.7,en-US;q=0.628 at (90.3%) OR zh-CN,zh;q=0.83 at (9.7%) " zh-CN " means "Mainland Chinese" Language preference. " zh " just means any version of Chinese. For all 121 records observed for this AS there were 31 alternative language preference specified. This is an optional header, however the indication of a desired alternate language preference can narrow down our search scope considerably. I applied the filter as: http.request.accept-language : " zh-CN,zh;q=0.9,en;q=0.8,en-GB;q=0.7,en-US;q=0.6 " OR http.request.accept-language : " zh-CN,zh;q=0.8 " At this point I exported the 31 records for this filter: I took these records over to LibreOffice as a Tab Separated Value sheet so I could have a look at it. When I did the pattern was unmistakable: These are all regularly scanning internet hosts for the same set of endpoints all from the same Canadian based AS-7456: 165[.]154.36.91 165[.]154.29.93 165[.]154.11.140 165[.]154.120.226 165[.]154.33.72 165[.]154.182.221 Values for http.request.body.content were all consistent repetitions of: /cgi-bin/login /config.json /sitemap.xml /robots.txt /favicon.ico / There is no attempt being made to conceal the fact that these user agents strongly desire Chinese character sets in the HTTP Language preferences while actively targeting internet facing endpoints. We have discovered an obviously automated campaign. Interestingly, tzrhxln[.]cn ( 165[.]154.29.93 ) is a suspect high entropy domain. Similar domains also appear in this dataset as extracted with this ESQL Query: source.domain values: leheedu[.]cn mail.,brossy.com[.]cn mail.brossy.com[.]cn tzrhxln[.]cn All of these domains operate from AS-7456, have strong CN presence, and are actively scanning. One Conclusion This demonstration of a simple approach to Elastic Discovery using optional HTTP language preferences and mime types is only an example. We have found high entropy domains, bot scanners, and plenty of nefarious intent, however the most interesting aspect in my view is the approach we have taken. Expanding upon this could yield automation. Typically, when analyzing datasets in a SIEM it is common to look for all the fields that match a correlation. In this approach we attempt to match the least commonality required to gain a single insight into what hosts may be related and then repeat the data acquisition process with this selected feature. This is featuring selection, and because we are purposely iterating upon the selection with intent, we are functionally engaged in rudimentary feature engineering. Using the embedded language preferences in webtraffic as a starting point we were able to trim a massive corpus into a manageable selection. We have also built upon some understanding of how these language headers appear in logs when browsing, so we could always simply begin selecting those features as a starting point in the future when processing SIEM data. Just a simple example for today, but we eventually found what we were looking for. Also, most importantly, the more efficient we are in the search, then the more time we have for our coffee. article.title: Siemens Mendix SAML Module
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Mendix SAML module contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to gain unauthorized access by replaying a valid SAML assertion in IdP-initiated authentication flows. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. The following versions of Siemens Mendix SAML Module are affected: Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) vers:intdot/ Mendix SAML (Mendix 11 compatible) vers:intdot/ Mendix SAML (Mendix 9 compatible) vers:intdot/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 6.8 Siemens Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) 1 Vulnerability Authentication Bypass by Capture-replay Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-89209 Affected versions of the module do not properly protect against SAML assertion replay in IdP-initiated authentication flows. This could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to gain unauthorized access to the application by replaying a valid SAML response. Read More 3 Affected Products Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Disable IdP-initiated SSO Vendor fix Update to V4.2.4 or later version Mendix SAML (Mendix 11 compatible) Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Disable IdP-initiated SSO Vendor fix Update to V4.2.4 or later version Mendix
article.raw_text: Siemens Mendix SAML Module View CSAF Summary Mendix SAML module contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to gain unauthorized access by replaying a valid SAML assertion in IdP-initiated authentication flows. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. The following versions of Siemens Mendix SAML Module are affected: Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) vers:intdot/ Mendix SAML (Mendix 11 compatible) vers:intdot/ Mendix SAML (Mendix 9 compatible) vers:intdot/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 6.8 Siemens Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) 1 Vulnerability Authentication Bypass by Capture-replay Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-89209 Affected versions of the module do not properly protect against SAML assertion replay in IdP-initiated authentication flows. This could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to gain unauthorized access to the application by replaying a valid SAML response. Read More 3 Affected Products Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Disable IdP-initiated SSO Vendor fix Update to V4.2.4 or later version Mendix SAML (Mendix 11 compatible) Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Disable IdP-initiated SSO Vendor fix Update to V4.2.4 or later version Mendix SAML (Mendix 9 compatible) Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Disable IdP-initiated SSO Vendor fix Update to V3.6.29 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-294 Authentication Bypass by Capture-replay CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 6.8 MEDIUM CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet . Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics . Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies . CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets . Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies . Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. article.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-48356 Adobe Commerce and Magento Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability CVE-2026-111497 Google Brotli Unchecked Return Value Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. article.title: The Gentlemen: A closer look at a not-so-gentle ransomware-as-a-service operation
article.summary: Our Threat Research Unit published a breakdown of “The Gentlemen” - a Russian-speaking ransomware-as-a-service group that emerged in mid-2025, reportedly after affiliates split off from established groups like LockBit and Qilin. A few things that stood out from the research: They’re offering affiliates up to 90% of ransom revenue - aggressive even by RaaS standards Claimed 800+ victims across the US and Europe, making them one of the top RaaS groups this year Cross-platform ransomware variants targeting Windows, Linux, NAS, and BSD Active use of EDR-killing tooling - one recent incident involved a custom dropper abusing vulnerable Safetica ProcessMonitor and Lenovo BootRepair.sys drivers (BYOVD) A breach of the group’s own infrastructure gave researchers rare visibility into their affiliate network, tooling, and ties to the broader ransomware ecosystem Full technical writeup linked below for anyone who wants to dig into the IOCs and affiliate details. https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/the-gentlemen-a-closer-look-at-a-not-so-gentle-ransomware-as-a-service-operation/ submitted by /u/acronis [link] [comments]

article.title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
article.summary: The self-deleting VOLTA infostealer steals credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets. Then, it uses LLMs to profile victims and rank their most valuable assets.
article.raw_text: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer The self-deleting VOLTA infostealer steals credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets. Then, it uses LLMs to profile victims and rank their most valuable assets. VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails. This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator. There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort , is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage. After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token. The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets. Figure 1. The VOLTA-AUTODOXER workflow. The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.” VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models. Endpoint https[ :]// openrouter [ .]ai/ api /v1/chat/completions Default model anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 Fallback chain moonshotai /kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash Temperature 0.2 — deterministic, consistent output Request format Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 Figure 2. Hardcoded model selection. Figure 3. Failover model selection to kimi-k2, and then gemini-2.5-flash. Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models. The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations. Figure 4. VOLTA's raw system prompt. The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped. Stealer capabilities VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report. Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext. Figure 5. VOLTA dumps plaintext passwords for every saved Wi-Fi network on the host. Figure 6. The organized collection targets. What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup. Figure 7. That’s right: Your Uber Eats history is now a potential liability. After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”. Figure 8. VOLTA’s exfil can happen in three stages: 1) after the stealer runs (“volta_log.zip”), 2) after the AI call (“volta_dox.zip”), (3) if the network enrichment produces anything (“volta_doxnet.zip”). The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated. Deployment model Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time. This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them. If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox. All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure. Countermeasures Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply. In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device. Conclusions VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM , though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next. Figure 9. End-to-end VOLTA workflow. The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement. The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself. hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on vectors: phishing, vpn-edge, credential-theft; impact: data-breach, fraud.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('battle.net','hide.me','rolimons.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Data staging and exfiltration to attacker-controlled storage
hypotheses.statement: Sensitive data has been staged (archived) and exfiltrated to attacker-controlled endpoints or cloud-storage tenants in the reporting window.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'exfiltration' selected based on vectors: phishing, vpn-edge, credential-theft; impact: data-breach, fraud.

objectives.title: Cloud-storage exfil to non-corp tenants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If DLP / proxy show no uploads to mega.nz, anonfiles, transfer.sh, or personal Dropbox/OneDrive tenants, cloud exfil is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: proxy | where host matches /mega\.nz|anonfiles\.com|transfer\.sh|filebin\.net/ | summarize bytes = sum(bytes_out) by user

objectives.title: Archive-then-egress pattern
objectives.falsification_criterion: If user/host telemetry shows no archive creation (rar/7z) within minutes of a large outbound transfer, the stage-then-exfil pattern is absent.
objectives.suggested_query: file_create | where ext in ('.rar','.7z','.zip') | join (egress | where bytes_out > 50MB) on host within 30m

objectives.title: Outbound volume to rare ASNs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If outbound bytes-by-ASN over the last 30 days show no first-seen / low-reputation destination receiving >1GB, bulk exfil is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: netflow | summarize bytes = sum(bytes_out) by asn | where asn !in (corp_known_asns) and bytes > 1GB

objectives.title: DNS-tunnelling search
objectives.falsification_criterion: If DNS query-length and txt-record distributions show no entropy / volume anomalies per source, DNS-tunnelled exfil is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | summarize avg(query_length), p99(query_length), count() by client_ip | where p99 > 200 and count() > 1000

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on vectors: phishing, vpn-edge, credential-theft; impact: data-breach, fraud.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: PHP Vulnerability Wrap-Up, (Fri, Oct 23rd)
article.summary: This morning, we returned to Infocon Green. As usual, we are raising the Infocon to alert you to emerging situations requiring immediate attention. PHP fit that description. By now, you either know about it, or you probably never will, so it is time to go back to "business as usual".
article.raw_text: PHP Vulnerability Wrap-Up, (Fri, Oct 23rd) This morning, we returned to Infocon Green. As usual, we are raising the Infocon to alert you to emerging situations requiring immediate attention. PHP fit that description. By now, you either know about it, or you probably never will, so it is time to go back to "business as usual". This morning, we returned to Infocon Green. As usual, we are raising the Infocon to alert you to emerging situations requiring immediate attention. PHP fit that description. By now, you either know about it, or you probably never will, so it is time to go back to "business as usual". Many vendors have released patches for the vulnerability in sync with PHP.net, showing that the coordinated vulnerability disclosure worked and achieved its goal of providing tested and working patches in a timely manner. Some vendor(s) not playing by the rules and leaking details early is unfortunate but should not overshadow the overall success of providing the patches. At this point, no reliable exploit has been made available publicly as far as I know. Several firms stated that they possess working exploit code, and I consider it a matter of time before such code becomes publicly available, at which point we will likely see more widespread exploitation. Cloudflare and Amazon have stated that they are seeing a large number of exploit attempts, but it is not clear if these are actual working exploits. Applying the patch remains your best and only reliable defense. Treat the time you have now as a gift and use it wisely to find and patch applications in your organization. If you are not able to upgrade, do your best to isolate vulnerable applications. There are various workarounds, but none are considered 100% effective. They may buy you more time. The same is true for web application firewall rules. As so often, embedded devices and appliances are a major concern, and many of them have not been updated or are unlikely to ever receive a patch. These types of devices should be isolated regardless. The PHP issue is likely just one of many weaknesses that could be exploited. Router admin interfaces, network storage devices, cameras, cat feeding stations, and refrigerators should not be exposed to the internet, and should be isolated on internal networks. At this point, this is table stakes regardless if they are running PHP. This vulnerability is also a good "dress rehearsal" of what is likely going to come. Vulnerability disclosure worked in this case. Patches were available. There will likely be many more vulnerabilities of similar severity that will be released and exploited with less responsibility. Be ready, run your tabletop exercises, update your inventories... Many partial exploits have been released. Be careful; some of them may be "parasitic," trying to exploit whoever runs them. It may be hard to even identify the working exploit once it comes out. The vulnerability and the risk are real, even if we did not see immediate mass exploitation. That part is still to come; it is just delayed. Just like we lower our infocon, make sure to rest and disconnect a bit, and do not stay "on alert" for too long. You will need the strength for the next issue. And do not overlook other issues that may have been missed this week: Node.js, Fortinet ... and more -- Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu Twitter | (c) SANS Internet Storm Center. https://isc.sans.edu Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 United States License.

article.title: IDC MarketScape names Microsoft a Leader in the 2026 Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises Vendor Assessment
article.summary: IDC has named Microsoft a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises. The post IDC MarketScape names Microsoft a Leader in the 2026 Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises Vendor Assessment appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .
article.raw_text: IDC MarketScape names Microsoft a Leader in the 2026 Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises Vendor Assessment IDC has named Microsoft a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises. The post IDC MarketScape names Microsoft a Leader in the 2026 Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises Vendor Assessment appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog . Today, we’re proud to share thatMicrosoft has been named a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises (Doc #US54123526, September 2026). The IDC Marketscape calls out three strengths that we believe matter most in endpoint security today: Autonomous attack disruption and predictive shielding contain ransomware and identity attacks in minutes, at a meaningful scale. Agentic AI through Security Copilot is now generally available, with measured gains in alert accuracy and analyst time saved. The company offers broad native cross-platform coverage plus sovereign cloud and data residency options for regulated and multinational customers. Read the IDC report IDC MarketScape vendor analysis model is designed to provide an overview of the competitive fitness of technology and suppliers in a given market. The research methodology utilizes a rigorous scoring methodology based on both qualitative and quantitative criteria that results in a single graphical illustration of each supplier’s position within a given market. The Capabilities score measures supplier product, go-to-market and business execution in the short-term. The Strategy score measures alignment of supplier strategies with customer requirements in a 3-5-year timeframe. Supplier market share is represented by the size of the icons. The most critical moment in any attack is when it moves from access to action. That’s when ransomware detonates, stolen credentials are put to work, and, increasingly, a manipulated AI agent turns a user’s own data and tools against them. And threat actors are now using teams of AI agents to execute attacks faster and more relentlessly. Between 2025 and 2026, Microsoft Security researchers observed a more than 15% increase in ransomware detonations against enterprises. 1 When an attacker can move from first foothold to encryption in minutes, protection on the endpoint must act at the same speed, without waiting for a person to connect the dots. Protection that acts while the attack is still unfolding The IDC MarketScape highlights that “Automatic attack disruption contains compromised devices, users, and IP addresses in near real time, and predictive shielding proactively hardens likely next attacker moves.” Built into Microsoft Defender , attack disruption uses AI and signals from the endpoint and across identities, email, and cloud to recognize multistage attacks, such as ransomware, as they happen. It then automatically contains the affected devices and users to stop the attacker from moving laterally. Against attacks that move in minutes, protection has to work autonomously, while the attack is still in progress and before it can spread. QNET, a global direct-selling company, saw this firsthand. Defender identified an active ransomware attack, isolated the compromised device, and stopped the second-stage payload within 128 seconds of the first high-severity alert . A foundation built for agentic security Stopping an attack like QNET’s in seconds starts with the right foundation. Attack disruption succeeds because Defender can see activity across endpoints, identities, email, and cloud, understand what that activity means, and act on it natively. The IDC MarketScape highlights that “the Defender portal unifies incident and alert queues, graph-based incident views, and advanced hunting, correlating signals from endpoint, identity, email, SaaS, and cloud sources into a single incident.” That foundation depends on three layers working as one. Signals and sensors give the system awareness across the entire environment. Context turns those signals into understanding: what is happening, what is exposed, how an attacker could move, and what matters most. Actuators, like attack disruption, turn that understanding into protective action. To protect against the latest AI-based threats, these layers need to work in unison. That’s why, on September 23, 2026, we announced the integrated security operations center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender . ISOC brings security information and event management (SIEM) and Defender’s threat protection together, giving people and agents shared signals, shared context, and shared controls to see, understand, and act across the environment as one. On top of that foundation, we continue to strengthen what Defender can see: Richer endpoint signals: Defender provides more than 200 native event types for threat hunting. Custom data collection extends that visibility by letting security teams collect specialized telemetry to support tailored detections and advanced hunting. Comprehensive signals across your environment: Microsoft Sentinel now provides more than 500 connectors to ingest security-relevant data from across your organization’s digital estate. This breadth gives defenders the context to connect activity across otherwise fragmented systems, detect threats that no single signal would reveal, and investigate and respond with greater confidence. Agentic AI built into the flow of work With signals, context, and actuators working as one in Microsoft Defender, agents have what they need to be effective: the visibility to see what’s happening, the context to understand it, and the controls to act on it. IDC notes that AI is deeply embedded across the Defender platform, with agentic AI now generally available and delivering “measured gains in alert accuracy and analyst time saved.” One platform to see, understand, and protect local AI agents The same visibility, context, and controls that make agents effective for defenders also make it possible to secure the agents employees use every day. Developers and knowledge workers now run local agents, from coding assistants to agentic development environments, with access to data, credentials, tools, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. IDC advises buyers to ask how vendors secure AI on the endpoint, including visibility into local models and agent activity. With Defender, security teams can see those agents, understand their reach, and protect them as they operate. See every local agent: Discovery of local agents and their configured MCP servers is available on Windows and macOS, covering more than 50 supported agents and MCP servers, including claw-based agents such as OpenClaw. Understand their reach: The exposure graph in Defender maps each agent’s blast radius across devices, identities, and MCP connections, and teams can investigate agent activity in advanced hunting alongside data from endpoints, identities, email, and cloud. Protect agents as they operate: Runtime protection, in preview on Windows, stops malicious instructions, such as prompt injection hidden in a file or web page, before an agent acts on them, and raises an alert with agent and session context. In a threat landscape being reshaped by AI, Microsoft Defender will continue to deliver leading endpoint security for any platform with a focus on reducing exposure, disrupting active attacks in your environment, and strengthening resilience across the entire organization. To see where security operations are headed next, join Rob Lefferts at Microsoft Ignite for the session: The Alert Is Dead. The Blueprint for the Agentic SOC. Microsoft named a Leader by IDC Read the 2026 IDC MarketScape to learn why IDC named Microsoft a Leader in Worldwide Modern Endpoint Security for Enterprises. Read the report To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on vectors: exploit, credential-theft; impact: ransomware, fraud.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('the published C2 domains') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Post-foothold lateral movement consistent with the reported actor
hypotheses.statement: An attacker who matched the TTPs of the reported actor has moved laterally inside the estate using RDP/SMB/WinRM, admin tooling, or Kerberos abuse.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'lateral_movement' selected based on vectors: exploit, credential-theft; impact: ransomware, fraud.

objectives.title: Anomalous remote logons (Type 3 / Type 10)
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4624 logon-type 3/10 events show no bursts from a single source to many destinations, lateral movement via RDP/SMB is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id in (4624) and logon_type in (3,10) | summarize dests = dcount(dst_host) by src_user, src_host | where dests > 10

objectives.title: Admin-tool usage outside baseline
objectives.falsification_criterion: If PsExec / WMIC / PowerShell remoting / Impacket-style usage is absent outside known admin jump-hosts, the lateral-tool hypothesis is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('psexec.exe','psexesvc.exe','wmic.exe','wsmprovhost.exe') and host !in (admin_jumphosts)

objectives.title: Kerberos abuse telemetry
objectives.falsification_criterion: If 4769 ticket requests show no anomalous RC4 / odd-SPN patterns and no AS-REP roasting indicators, credential-based lateral movement is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: security | where event_id == 4769 and ticket_encryption == 'RC4-HMAC' | summarize by target_spn, account_name

objectives.title: Lateral file-copy staging
objectives.falsification_criterion: If SMB writes of archives / executables across multiple hosts from one user/host are absent, lateral staging is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: file | where action == 'write' and ext in ('.7z','.rar','.zip','.exe') and dest matches /\\\\.*\\(C\$|admin\$)/

article.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-27834 Apple Multiple Products Improper Authentication Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nominati

objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'Ivanti Connect Secure' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-111357 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-111357/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-111357 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-111357')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on Ivanti Connect Secure hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; products: Ivanti Connect Secure.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('the published C2 domains') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-111357, CVE-2026-118527; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge; products: Ivanti Connect Secure.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-110447 Collabora Online – Built-in CODE Server OS Command Injection Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’

objectives.title: Cloud-storage exfil to non-corp tenants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If DLP / proxy show no uploads to mega.nz, anonfiles, transfer.sh, or personal Dropbox/OneDrive tenants, cloud exfil is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: proxy | where host matches /mega\.nz|anonfiles\.com|transfer\.sh|filebin\.net/ | summarize bytes = sum(bytes_out) by user

objectives.title: Archive-then-egress pattern
objectives.falsification_criterion: If user/host telemetry shows no archive creation (rar/7z) within minutes of a large outbound transfer, the stage-then-exfil pattern is absent.
objectives.suggested_query: file_create | where ext in ('.rar','.7z','.zip') | join (egress | where bytes_out > 50MB) on host within 30m

objectives.title: Outbound volume to rare ASNs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If outbound bytes-by-ASN over the last 30 days show no first-seen / low-reputation destination receiving >1GB, bulk exfil is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: netflow | summarize bytes = sum(bytes_out) by asn | where asn !in (corp_known_asns) and bytes > 1GB

objectives.title: DNS-tunnelling search
objectives.falsification_criterion: If DNS query-length and txt-record distributions show no entropy / volume anomalies per source, DNS-tunnelled exfil is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | summarize avg(query_length), p99(query_length), count() by client_ip | where p99 > 200 and count() > 1000
